sentence: When Paul writes that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law, he is not dismissing obedience but relocating its source. Righteousness, in his argument to the Romans, is reckoned to Abraham before circumcision and before the giving of the Torah, so that the promise might rest on grace. The believer is incorporated into Christ's death and raised with him, and from this union the fruit of the Spirit follows as consequence rather than precondition.

Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have obtained access into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame.

The tension between James and Paul on faith and works has occupied commentators for centuries. James insists that faith without works is dead, citing the same Abraham whom Paul makes the model of believing trust. Many resolve the apparent contradiction by noting that the two writers use the word works differently: Paul opposes works of the law as a boundary marker of covenant membership, while James condemns a barren profession that produces no love of neighbour.

Paul's letter to the Galatians treats the question with unusual heat, for he believes the gospel itself is at stake. To require the gentile converts to be circumcised is, in his judgment, to fall away from grace and to make Christ of no advantage. He recounts his confrontation with Peter at Antioch as a defence of the principle that no one is justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.

The phrase the righteousness of God in Romans has generated a long exegetical debate. Some readers take it as an attribute of God, his own covenant faithfulness; others take it as a status God confers upon the believer. The Reformation tradition emphasised the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith, while more recent scholarship has stressed the covenantal and forensic dimensions together, reading the term against the background of Israel's scriptures.

For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. The Ephesian passage thus holds together the denial of meritorious works and the affirmation of works as the purpose of the new creation.

Paul's argument in Romans builds toward the claim that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. The cross is presented as the place where God demonstrates his righteousness, having passed over former sins in his forbearance. The atonement is therefore not a device by which mercy overrides justice but the means by which both are upheld at once.

Augustine read Paul against the Pelagians and found in the epistles a doctrine of grace that precedes and enables every good act of the will. The human person, wounded by sin, cannot will the good without the prior healing of divine love. Later interpreters who departed from this reading were nonetheless compelled to engage Paul's insistence that what we have, we have received, and that boasting is therefore excluded.

What then shall we say? That gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law. Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone.

The new perspective on Paul has argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of works-righteousness but of covenant grace, so that Paul's polemic must be understood as addressing the inclusion of gentiles rather than the problem of human merit. Critics reply that Paul's language about boasting and about the inability of the law to give life points to a deeper anthropological problem than the question of ethnic boundary alone.

The science of tajwid governs the precise articulation of the Quran, specifying for each letter its point of origin in the mouth and throat and the qualities of breath and resonance that distinguish it. A reciter who lengthens a vowel must hold it for the prescribed count, and the rules of assimilation and nasalisation transform the sounds where certain letters meet, so that the recitation preserves the form in which the revelation was received.

Recite the Quran with measured recitation, the revelation instructs, and the commentators have understood this command as the foundation of tartil, the unhurried and attentive mode of reading. To rush through the verses is to neglect the meanings and to slur the letters; to recite slowly is to give each word its right and to allow the heart to dwell on what the tongue pronounces.

The seven canonical readings transmitted from the early reciters preserve minor variations in vocalisation and occasionally in consonantal text, all of which the tradition regards as part of the revelation given in seven modes. A student trained in the reading of Hafs from Asim recites the Quran differently in certain words from one trained in the reading of Warsh from Nafi, and each chain of transmission is documented back through named teachers to the Prophet.

When the silent letter nun or the nunation meets one of the throat letters, it is pronounced clearly without nasal resonance, but when it meets the letters of assimilation it merges into the following sound. These rules, memorised by every student of recitation, are not arbitrary ornament but the means of guarding the oral transmission against drift, since a fixed sound resists alteration in a way that a written sign alone cannot.

The places of pause and continuation in the Quranic text are themselves a subject of careful study, for to stop at the wrong word may distort the sense. Marks in the printed copies advise the reciter where a pause is obligatory, where it is permitted, and where it is forbidden, and a skilled reader weighs these against the grammar and meaning so that the recitation never severs a phrase from its completion.

The opening chapter, recited in every unit of the daily prayer, demands particular care in its articulation. The reciter distinguishes the heavy and light letters, gives the doubled consonants their full weight, and observes the prolongation in the final word so that the prayer is offered in the form the tradition has guarded. To pray without attention to these distinctions is permitted, but the masters teach that beauty in recitation is itself an act of reverence.

The Prophet is reported to have said that the one who recites the Quran skilfully will be in the company of the noble and righteous angels, and that the one who recites it with difficulty, stumbling over it, will have a double reward. The tradition thus honours both mastery and effort, and it encourages the beginner not to abandon recitation because of the labour it costs.

Prolongation in recitation falls into degrees, the natural lengthening of two counts and the longer stretches required when a long vowel is followed by a glottal stop or a doubled letter. The reciter who has internalised these measures need not count consciously, for the practised ear regulates the duration, much as a singer holds a note without measuring it. The discipline aims at a recitation that is neither hurried nor distended.

The traditional method of teaching recitation pairs the student with a teacher who has himself received an unbroken chain of authorisation, and the student does not merely read the text but reproduces the sound of his teacher's recitation. When the teacher judges the student to have mastered the whole, he grants a licence naming the chain of transmitters, and the student in turn becomes a link by which the recitation passes to the next generation.

The hidden nasalisation, in which the silent nun is partially merged with the following letter while a trace of resonance remains, is among the rules most difficult for the beginner to perform precisely. The masters describe it as a sound held between full clarity and full assimilation, and they insist that it be sustained for the correct duration, neither cut short nor stretched into a hum.

Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, form is not other than emptiness. So too feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty. The Heart Sutra presses this teaching to its farthest reach, declaring that in emptiness there is no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind, and finally no path, no wisdom, and no attainment, since there is nothing to be attained.

The Perfection of Wisdom literature teaches that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence, arising in dependence on causes and conditions and on the conceptual designations the mind imposes. To grasp emptiness is not to deny the appearances of the world but to see that they do not stand on their own; the practitioner who realises this is freed from the clinging that takes the conditioned for the absolute.

Subhuti, the Buddha says in the Diamond Sutra, a bodhisattva who is generous should give without abiding in the notion of a self that gives, a recipient who receives, or a gift that is given. One who practises generosity in this way, free of attachment to signs, accumulates merit as vast as the space of the eastern quarter, immeasurable and beyond reckoning.

Nagarjuna's verses on the middle way argue that whatever is dependently arisen is what is called emptiness, and that emptiness, being a dependent designation, is itself the middle way. Nothing exists that is not dependently arisen; therefore nothing exists that is not empty. The argument is not nihilism, for Nagarjuna insists that it is precisely because things are empty that the four noble truths and the path are possible.

All conditioned things are like a dream, a phantom, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and like lightning; thus should one contemplate them. With these images the Diamond Sutra closes its teaching, urging the practitioner to regard every compounded thing as fleeting and insubstantial, so that the mind neither grasps appearances nor rests in the bare denial of them.

The teaching of emptiness is sometimes likened to a raft. The Buddha tells those who have crossed the river that they should not carry the raft on their shoulders out of attachment to it, for its purpose was the crossing. So too the doctrine of emptiness is a means of release, and one who turns it into a fixed view to be defended has mistaken the medicine for a possession.

The Lankavatara Sutra warns against grasping emptiness as a thing in itself, calling those who do so incurable. Emptiness, it teaches, is not a void to be apprehended but the absence of the imagined self-nature that the deluded mind projects onto experience. The remedy for clinging to existence is the teaching of emptiness, but one who then clings to emptiness has fallen into a subtler error.

The two truths doctrine distinguishes conventional truth, in which persons act, ripen karma, and tread the path, from ultimate truth, in which no phenomenon is found to possess inherent existence. The teaching of emptiness belongs to the ultimate, yet it does not abolish the conventional; rather it grounds it, for only what is empty can change, and only what changes can be liberated.

In the Vimalakirti Sutra the layman Vimalakirti, when asked by the assembled bodhisattvas to expound the gate of nonduality, answers with silence. Manjushri praises this response, for in it there are no words, no syllables, no display of any teaching, and the assembly understands that the deepest expression of emptiness cannot be captured in speech and is shown most fully where speech ceases.

Because there is no self to be defended and no possession to be lost, the practitioner who understands emptiness can act in the world with fearless compassion. The Perfection of Wisdom teaches that the bodhisattva, seeing that beings are empty and yet labouring under the false belief in their own substantiality, is moved to liberate them, and that this compassion arising from wisdom is the heart of the great vehicle.

The Mishnah records that the schools of Hillel and Shammai disagreed for three years, each insisting that the law followed its own ruling, until a heavenly voice declared that both are the words of the living God but the law follows the school of Hillel. The Talmud asks why Hillel prevailed and answers that his disciples were gentle and modest, studying both their own opinions and those of their opponents, and even citing the rulings of Shammai before their own.

In the dispute over the oven of Akhnai, Rabbi Eliezer summoned miracles to support his ruling, and a carob tree moved, a stream flowed backward, and a heavenly voice proclaimed that the law was as he said. But Rabbi Joshua rose and declared that the Torah is not in heaven, for it was given at Sinai and is no longer subject to a heavenly voice; the law is decided by the majority of the sages, and the tradition reports that God smiled and said his children had defeated him.

The Talmudic method preserves the rejected opinion alongside the accepted one, recording the reasoning of the minority so that future generations may study it. The rabbis explain that a minority view is not deleted from the record because circumstances may arise in which a court will rely upon it, and because the discipline of weighing both sides is itself the substance of Torah study.

A dispute is for the sake of heaven, the sages teach, if it resembles the disputes of Hillel and Shammai, and such a dispute will endure; a dispute not for the sake of heaven, like that of Korah and his company, will not endure. The distinction lies not in the agreement reached but in the motive of the disputants, for the argument pursued in the search for truth has lasting value even when it is not resolved.

The Gemara frequently raises an objection against a stated ruling by citing a contradictory teaching, and then resolves the tension by distinguishing the cases, by attributing the two statements to different authorities, or by emending the wording of one source. This dialectical movement, repeated across the tractates, trains the student to hold several positions in mind at once and to seek the precise condition under which each holds.

When the sages could not determine the law by reasoning, they sometimes ruled according to established custom, declaring that one should go out and see what the people are doing. In other cases an undecided question was left with the word teyku, which the tradition reads as an acronym indicating that the prophet Elijah will resolve all difficulties at the end of days, so that the unanswered question is not erased but suspended.

The principle that the law follows the majority is derived from a verse instructing that one should incline after the multitude. The rabbis apply this rule both to courts ruling on a case and to the assembled sages determining a general law, and they hold that even a single dissenting authority of great learning must yield to the count of voices, for the alternative is endless division.

Rabbi Eliezer, after the oven of Akhnai, was placed under a ban by the other sages, and the Talmud relates the grief of that day, when the produce of the fields was struck and the world suffered for the wound to a great teacher. The episode is told not to vindicate the ban but to record its cost, and the tradition holds in tension the necessity of communal decision and the honour due to the one who is overruled.

A teaching attributed to the sages holds that scholars who debate the law increase peace in the world, for the verse promises that all your children shall be taught of the Lord and great shall be the peace of your children. The rabbis read the word for children as builders, understanding that those who build through study and argument are the makers of peace, and that contention pursued for understanding is not the enemy of harmony but its foundation.

When two verses appear to contradict each other, the rabbis teach, a third verse must be sought that reconciles them. This hermeneutical rule, one of the thirteen principles of interpretation attributed to Rabbi Ishmael, governs much of the legal argument of the Talmud, for the sages assume that the Torah does not contradict itself and that an apparent clash signals an unnoticed distinction waiting to be uncovered.

In the Chandogya Upanishad the father instructs his son to dissolve salt in water and then to taste the water at its surface, its middle, and its depths, finding it salt everywhere though the salt itself is unseen. So, the father says, the subtle essence pervades all that is, and that essence is the self of all; that thou art, he tells him, and the teaching is repeated until the truth is fixed in the listening mind.

The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad teaches that the self is to be known through the negation of every limiting description, for it is not this, not this. Whatever the mind names, the self exceeds; it is the witness behind all seeing, the hearer behind all hearing, the knower who cannot be made an object of knowledge. The sage who realises this is no longer bound by name and form.

Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality. This prayer of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad gathers the aspiration of the seeker into three movements, asking not for possessions but for passage from illusion to truth, from ignorance to wisdom, and from the perishing condition to the deathless ground that the teaching identifies with the innermost self.

The Mandukya Upanishad analyses the syllable Om into its three sounds and a fourth silent measure, correlating them with the waking, dreaming, and deep-sleep states and with the fourth, the pure consciousness that underlies them all. The fourth is described as not inwardly cognitive, not outwardly cognitive, beyond all designation, the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful and nondual, and it is declared to be the self that is to be known.

The Katha Upanishad sets the teaching of immortality in a dialogue between the boy Nachiketa and Death himself. Death offers wealth and long life and the pleasures of the world, but the boy refuses them all, asking only to know what lies beyond death. The teaching that follows compares the self to the rider of a chariot, the body to the chariot, the intellect to the charioteer, and the senses to the horses that must be governed.

Two birds, companions always united, cling to the selfsame tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating. The Mundaka Upanishad uses this image to distinguish the individual self caught in the experience of pleasure and sorrow from the supreme self that abides as the unmoved witness, and it teaches that when the first beholds the second, its grief departs.

The Isha Upanishad opens with the declaration that all this, whatever moves in the moving world, is to be regarded as enveloped by the Lord. The verse counsels that one should therefore enjoy what is given through renunciation and not covet the wealth of any other, for the recognition that all is pervaded by the divine transforms possession into trust and grasping into release.

The Taittiriya Upanishad describes the self as composed of five sheaths, the body made of food, the vital breath, the mind, the discriminating intellect, and the sheath of bliss. The student is led inward from the outermost to the innermost, and at the centre the teaching places not a further sheath but the ground of bliss itself, from which all beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return.

The great sayings of the Upanishads condense the teaching into a few words. One declares that consciousness is the absolute; another that this self is the absolute; another that the absolute alone exists. The tradition treats these as the seeds from which the whole instruction unfolds, and the seeker is told to hear them, to reflect upon them, and to meditate until the truth they announce is no longer a statement but a realisation.

When the Svetasvatara Upanishad asks what the cause is, whether it is time, or nature, or necessity, or chance, or the elements, it answers that the seekers, absorbed in meditation, beheld the power of the divine self hidden by its own qualities. The text moves from cosmological speculation to the inner discipline by which the hidden ground is uncovered, teaching that the cause sought outwardly is found within.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning? O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest. Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel. In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them. The psalm moves from the cry of abandonment to the memory of past deliverance.

Out of the depths I cry to you, O Lord. Lord, hear my voice; let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy. If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared. I wait for the Lord, my soul waits, and in his word I hope; my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning.

The lament psalms follow a recognisable pattern, opening with an address to God and a complaint, moving to petition and to reasons God should act, and frequently turning at the end to an expression of trust or a vow of praise. Interpreters have noted that this turn, often abrupt, suggests that the act of crying out before God is itself the path by which the worshipper passes from despair toward hope.

Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits, who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy. As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.

How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? Consider and answer me, O Lord my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death. But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation.

The hymns of praise in the Psalter call the whole creation to worship, summoning the sun and moon, the sea creatures and the deeps, the mountains and the cattle, the kings of the earth and all peoples. This widening summons reflects a conviction that praise is the proper response of every creature to its maker, and that the worshipper who joins the chorus is taking up a role assigned in the order of things.

Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. The penitential psalm pleads not merely for pardon but for inward renewal, asking that the heart itself be remade.

Some psalms of lament voice not personal distress but the grief of the whole community, recalling national defeat or exile. By the rivers of Babylon, one such psalm begins, there we sat down and wept when we remembered Zion. The communal lament gives ritual form to collective sorrow, and its inclusion in worship allowed a people to bring even its catastrophes into the presence of God rather than leaving them unspoken.

Praise the Lord! Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens. Praise him for his mighty deeds; praise him according to his excellent greatness. Praise him with trumpet sound; praise him with lute and harp. Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. The final psalm closes the Psalter with an unbroken summons to praise, naming the instruments and ending with the whole of breathing creation.

Many psalms of lament protest the prosperity of the wicked and the suffering of the faithful, pressing the question of divine justice. One such psalm confesses that the worshipper had nearly stumbled, envying the arrogant, until he went into the sanctuary of God and discerned their end. The complaint is not silenced but reframed, the worshipper's perspective enlarged by an encounter that does not abolish the difficulty but sets it within a longer view.

There is one supreme being, the eternal reality, the creator, without fear, without enmity, timeless in form, beyond birth, self-existent, known by the grace of the Guru. The opening words of the Guru Granth Sahib gather the central affirmations of the Sikh faith into a single statement, beginning with the numeral one and the name of the formless divine, and the verses that follow unfold this declaration into the Japji of Guru Nanak.

By thinking, the divine cannot be reduced to thought, even if one thinks a hundred thousand times. By remaining silent, inner silence is not obtained, even if one remains absorbed in trance. The hunger of the hungry is not satisfied, even by piling up the loads of the world. Guru Nanak asks in the Japji how then one may become true and break the wall of falsehood, and he answers that it is by walking in the will of the divine.

The hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are arranged according to the musical measures in which they are to be sung, so that the scripture is at once a text and a body of devotional music. Each measure carries its own mood, and the tradition holds that the singing of the word in its appointed measure draws the mind into the remembrance of the divine name more surely than recitation alone.

The scripture teaches that the divine name is the remedy for the wandering and self-centred mind. He who keeps the name in the heart, the verses declare, is freed from the cycle of coming and going, and his life is fruitful. The repetition of the name is not a mechanical act but the orientation of the whole person toward the one reality, and the Guru is the door through which this remembrance is learned.

The Guru Granth Sahib gathers the compositions not only of the Sikh Gurus but also of saints from beyond the Sikh community, including the weaver Kabir and the cobbler Ravidas, whose hymns sit within the scripture on the same footing as the Gurus' own. This inclusion expresses the conviction that the divine word may be uttered through any sincere devotee, regardless of caste or creed, and that truth is not the possession of one tradition.

Why should I do good deeds for the sake of reward, a hymn of Guru Arjan asks, and answers that the true devotee serves not to be paid but out of love. The scripture distinguishes the worship that bargains with the divine from the worship that asks nothing, and it places the second far above the first, teaching that the highest reward is the gift of the name itself.

The closing portion of the Japji compares the spiritual journey to five realms through which the seeker ascends, the realms of duty, of knowledge, of effort, of grace, and finally of truth. In the last realm the formless one dwells, and there the seeker beholds the order of all the worlds and is absorbed in the joy of beholding. The composition ends not with a possession attained but with a contemplation that has no end.

The scripture is treated by the Sikh community as the living embodiment of the Guru, installed in the place of worship with honour, opened and read each day, and consulted for guidance. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, ended the line of human Gurus by conferring guruship upon the scripture itself, so that the Sikhs would thereafter look to the word rather than to a person for their teaching.

As fragrance dwells within the flower and reflection within the mirror, so the divine dwells within, and is sought outside; the deluded one wanders, deceived by doubt. The hymn of the ninth Guru turns the seeker inward, teaching that the reality pursued through pilgrimage and ritual is already present in the heart, and that the Guru's word is the means by which this nearness is recognised.

The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that the householder's life, lived honestly and in remembrance of the divine, is a higher path than the renunciation of the world. One should earn by honest labour, share with the needy, and keep the name in the heart; this threefold practice, the scripture holds, sanctifies ordinary life and makes the home itself a place of devotion.

You have heard that it was said, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you, do not resist the one who is evil. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles.

Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. The beatitudes open the discourse by pronouncing favour upon those whom the world counts least, reversing the ordinary measure of blessing.

The teaching on the inward law intensifies the commandments rather than relaxing them. It is not enough not to murder, for anyone who is angry with his brother is liable to judgment; it is not enough not to commit adultery, for everyone who looks with lustful intent has already committed it in his heart. The sermon locates moral failure in the disposition and not only in the deed.

Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. No one can serve two masters; you cannot serve God and money. The sermon makes the orientation of desire the decisive question of the moral life.

Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye but do not notice the log in your own eye? The teaching does not forbid all discernment but warns against the self-deceived severity that condemns in others what it overlooks in itself.

When you pray, the sermon instructs, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret, and do not heap up empty phrases as the pagans do. The model prayer that follows is brief, asking that the divine name be hallowed, the kingdom come, daily bread be given, debts forgiven as the one praying forgives, and the one praying delivered from the time of trial.

Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. The sermon ends with a series of such contrasts, dividing not by profession but by practice, since not everyone who says Lord, Lord will enter the kingdom.

Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. The command grounds its demand in the character of God, whose generosity does not discriminate, and it asks the disciple to imitate that indiscriminate love.

Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. The discourse closes by making the doing of its teaching, and not merely the hearing, the test of a life that endures.

Therefore do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. The sermon counsels a freedom from anxiety grounded in trust, urging that the disciple seek first the kingdom and let each day's trouble be sufficient for the day.

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand. The prophet opens his book by summoning the cosmos as witness to a covenant lawsuit, charging the people with an ingratitude the dumb beasts do not share.

Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. The prophet Amos delivers this demand against a people that keeps the festivals and offers sacrifices while trampling the poor and turning aside the needy at the gate. The oracle declares that God despises the assemblies and will not accept the offerings, for the worship that ignores justice is an offence rather than a service.

Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land. The prophet pronounces a series of woes against the accumulation of property, the drunkenness that begins early in the day, and the calling of evil good and good evil, naming each social disorder as a wound that draws down judgment.

The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: stand in the gate of the Lord's house and proclaim there this word. Do not trust in these deceptive words, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord. For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, then I will let you dwell in this place. The oracle attacks the false security that treats the sanctuary as a guarantee.

The prophet Hosea casts the broken covenant as a marriage betrayed, and the oracle of judgment is shot through with the language of a wounded love. There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, the prophet declares, and no knowledge of God in the land; there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery. Yet within the same book the judgment is interrupted by the cry of a God who asks how he can give up his people.

The day of the Lord, the prophet warns, is darkness and not light, as if a man fled from a lion and a bear met him, or went into the house and leaned his hand against the wall and a serpent bit him. The oracle overturns the popular expectation that the coming day would bring vindication, declaring instead that it will fall heaviest on those who presumed upon it.

Ezekiel is shown a vision of the abominations in the temple and told that the glory of the Lord will depart from the sanctuary. The oracle of judgment is enacted as well as spoken, for the prophet is commanded to lie bound on his side for many days, to eat measured bread, and to shave his head, each sign-act dramatising the siege and exile that the words announce.

With what shall I come before the Lord, and bow myself before God on high? Shall I come with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? The prophet Micah poses the question and answers it: he has told you, O man, what is good, and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God. The oracle reduces the whole demand of the covenant to three clauses.

The prophets characteristically follow the announcement of judgment with the promise of a remnant, a small portion that will survive the catastrophe and become the seed of renewal. The judgment is therefore not the final word but a refining fire, and the oracle that threatens destruction often turns, sometimes within a single chapter, toward the vision of a purified people gathered again.

Your hands are full of blood, the prophet declares; wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes, cease to do evil, learn to do good, seek justice, correct oppression, bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause. Come now, let us reason together: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. The oracle of judgment opens unexpectedly into an offer of cleansing.

Origen taught that scripture has a body, a soul, and a spirit, and that just as the human being is composed of these three, so the divine writings yield a literal sense, a moral sense, and a spiritual sense. The simple reader is fed by the letter, the one who has made some progress by the soul, and the perfect by the spiritual law that contains a shadow of the good things to come.

Augustine, expounding the opening of Genesis, warned that the interpreter must not cling so firmly to a particular reading of the literal sense that, when fuller knowledge corrects it, the faith itself is brought into disrepute. He held that scripture accommodates itself to the capacities of its readers, and that where the letter seems to teach what is unworthy of God, the spiritual sense must be sought.

John Chrysostom, preaching through the epistle to the Romans, urged his congregation to read the scriptures at home and not to leave the study of them to the clergy alone. He compared the soul that neglects the word to a field left untilled, and he insisted that the obscurities of the text are themselves a providential goad, set there to make the reader labour and so to value what is found.

The school of Antioch, represented by Theodore of Mopsuestia, resisted the allegorical excesses of Alexandria and insisted on the historical sense of the text. Yet even the Antiochenes admitted a figural reading they called theoria, by which the prophet, while speaking of his own time, perceives a further fulfilment, so that the literal and the prophetic senses are held together rather than opposed.

Gregory the Great, commenting on the book of Job, treated the patriarch's afflictions as at once a record of historical suffering and a figure of the trials of the church and the soul. His method moved from the literal narrative to the moral lesson and then to the contemplative meaning, and he held that the same passage might nourish the reader differently according to the reader's stage of spiritual growth.

Jerome devoted his later years to translating the scriptures from the Hebrew, departing from the established Greek version because he held that the truth of the text must be sought in the original tongue. He defended this labour against critics who feared any change to the familiar wording, arguing that a translation true to the Hebrew would silence the objections of those who knew the source and could expose errors in the older renderings.

The fathers read the Old Testament as a book full of Christ, finding him prefigured in the paschal lamb, in the rock that gave water in the wilderness, and in the bronze serpent lifted up by Moses. This typological reading was not, in their understanding, an arbitrary imposition, for they believed the same God authored both Testaments and so wove the earlier history with foreshadowings of the later fulfilment.

Irenaeus, against the Gnostic teachers, insisted that the scriptures must be read within the rule of faith handed down in the churches, for a text severed from this rule could be twisted into any shape. He compared the heretics to one who takes a mosaic of a king and rearranges the same stones into the image of a dog, claiming the original was always meant to be a dog.

Basil of Caesarea delivered a series of homilies on the six days of creation, treating the Genesis account both as a true record of the world's making and as an occasion to praise the wisdom of the creator displayed in each ordered work. He drew on the natural knowledge of his age, but he subordinated it to the text, reading the creation narrative as a school in which the soul learns reverence.

The medieval division of the senses of scripture into the literal, the allegorical, the moral, and the anagogical was inherited from the fathers and condensed into a much-quoted couplet. The letter teaches the events, the allegory what one should believe, the moral sense what one should do, and the anagogical sense whither one is bound. The fourfold scheme summarised centuries of patristic practice in a form easily taught.

The Way that can be spoken of is not the constant Way; the name that can be named is not the constant name. The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things. So the opening of the Daodejing sets a paradox at the head of its teaching, for it commends a reality that withdraws from every word offered to capture it.

The highest good is like water, the Daodejing teaches, for water benefits the ten thousand things and does not contend, dwelling in places that people disdain. Therefore it is close to the Way. The classic repeatedly commends the yielding, the low, and the soft, holding that what is supple overcomes what is rigid and that the sage who does not strive is the one who cannot be opposed.

The Way does nothing, and yet there is nothing left undone. This is the heart of the teaching of wu-wei, action without forcing, which the Daodejing presents not as idleness but as a conduct aligned with the spontaneous course of things. The ruler who governs by wu-wei does not impose; he removes obstruction, and the people, the classic says, will believe they accomplished it of themselves.

Zhuangzi tells of dreaming that he was a butterfly, fluttering and content, knowing nothing of being Zhuangzi. Then he awoke and was unmistakably Zhuangzi. But he did not know whether he was Zhuangzi who had dreamt he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he was Zhuangzi. Between Zhuangzi and the butterfly there must be some distinction; this, he writes, is what is called the transformation of things.

Thirty spokes share one hub; it is the empty space that makes the wheel useful. Clay is shaped into a vessel; it is the hollow within that makes the vessel useful. Doors and windows are cut for a room; it is the empty space that makes the room useful. So the Daodejing teaches that what is present gives advantage, but it is what is absent that brings things to use.

Zhuangzi recounts the cook who carved an ox for many years and never dulled his blade, because he moved through the natural openings of the joints rather than hacking at the bone. The cook says that he no longer sees the ox with his eyes but meets it with his spirit, and the ruler who hears him declares that from the words of a cook he has learned the nurturing of life.

Knowing others is wisdom; knowing oneself is enlightenment. Mastering others requires force; mastering oneself requires strength. He who knows contentment is rich, and he who acts with persistence has will. So the Daodejing turns the measures of power inward, holding that the conquest worth seeking is the conquest of the self and that true wealth is found not in accumulation but in the cessation of craving.

When Zhuangzi was dying, his disciples wished to give him a lavish burial. He told them he would have heaven and earth for his coffin, the sun and moon for his jade ornaments, and the stars for his pearls; what funeral furnishings could be lacking? When they protested that crows would eat him, he replied that above ground the crows would eat him and below ground the ants would, and he asked why they would rob the one to feed the other.

The Daodejing warns the ruler against governing through cleverness and law, for the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people become; the sharper the weapons, the more disordered the state. It commends instead a government so light that the people scarcely know their ruler exists, and it teaches that the sage rules best who empties the people of restless ambition and fills them with what sustains.

Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know. The Daodejing turns its scepticism even upon itself, conceding that the written teaching falls short of the wordless reality it points toward. The reader is left with a paradox, for the classic commends silence in five thousand characters, and the tradition has read this not as contradiction but as an honest admission of the limits of language.

You have a right to your action alone, never to its fruits. Let not the fruits of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. So Krishna instructs Arjuna on the field of battle, teaching that the work itself must be done as a duty, with the mind released from anxious calculation of reward, for it is craving for the result that binds the soul.

Better one's own duty, though imperfectly performed, than the duty of another well performed. Better is death in the doing of one's own duty; the duty of another brings danger. Krishna presses upon Arjuna that the path appointed to each person, according to his nature and station, is the path he must walk, and that the imitation of another's role, however attractive, is a deviation that imperils the soul.

Arjuna lays down his bow, unwilling to fight against his kinsmen and teachers, and Krishna answers that the wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead. The embodied self, he teaches, is never born and never dies; as a person casts off worn garments and puts on new ones, so the self casts off worn bodies and enters others. The teaching of the imperishable self is the ground on which the call to duty is laid.

Krishna distinguishes three paths to liberation, the way of disinterested action, the way of knowledge, and the way of devotion, and he teaches that they are not rivals but converge. Action performed without attachment becomes a form of worship; knowledge purifies the doer; devotion offers every deed to the divine. The Gita weaves the three together so that the householder's duty itself becomes a discipline of release.

Whenever righteousness declines and unrighteousness rises, Krishna declares, then I send forth myself. For the protection of the good and the destruction of the wicked, for the establishment of righteousness, I am born from age to age. The Gita sets the call to duty within a vision of recurring divine descent, in which the cosmic order is restored when those who uphold it have grown few.

The one who is the same to friend and foe, the same in honour and dishonour, the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, free from attachment, to whom blame and praise are equal, content with whatever comes, having no fixed abode, steady of mind and full of devotion, that person, Krishna says to Arjuna, is dear to me. The Gita draws the portrait of the soul made even by discipline.

At the height of the teaching Krishna reveals his cosmic form, and Arjuna beholds the whole universe gathered in the body of the divine, with countless mouths and eyes, blazing like a thousand suns risen at once. Overwhelmed, Arjuna asks who this terrible form is, and the answer comes that it is Time, the destroyer of worlds, come to consume; the warrior's duty is set within a process already unfolding.

Abandoning all duties, Krishna says in the closing teaching, take refuge in me alone; I will release you from all sins, do not grieve. The verse has been read by some as the crown of the whole discourse, in which the way of devotion gathers up the way of action, for the deeds still to be done are now performed as a surrender, and the doer rests not in the outcome but in the divine to whom the deeds are given.

The disciplined soul, Krishna teaches, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, beholding the same everywhere. From this vision of unity a conduct follows that the Gita calls action without attachment, for one who recognises the single self in friend and stranger alike performs his appointed work as service rather than self-interest, and is not stained by what he does.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all ages, light from light, true God from true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things were made. The creed of Nicaea states the faith of the church against those who denied the full divinity of the Son.

The phrase of one substance with the Father was the decisive word at Nicaea, chosen because it could not be evaded by those who wished to call the Son divine in a lesser sense. Its critics objected that the term was not found in scripture, and the defenders replied that no single word of scripture could be set against the heretical reading, so that a precise term was needed to guard the biblical confession.

I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. The older baptismal confession structures the faith around the saving acts, naming the historical figure under whom the crucifixion took place so that the events are anchored in time.

The definition issued at Chalcedon confesses one and the same Christ, made known in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, the distinction of the natures being in no way removed by the union but rather the property of each nature preserved. The four negatives mark the boundaries within which the church held the mystery, ruling out both the mingling of the natures and their separation into two persons.

The Reformation produced confessions in which the churches set out their understanding of scripture at length. The Westminster Confession opens by affirming that the whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for salvation is either expressly set down in scripture or may be deduced from it by good and necessary consequence, and that nothing is to be added by new revelations or the traditions of men.

What is your only comfort in life and in death, the catechism of Heidelberg asks, and answers that it is that I am not my own, but belong with body and soul, both in life and in death, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. The confession is cast as a personal assurance, and the question-and-answer form was designed to be learned by heart so that the doctrine would be ready in the hour of trial.

The creed adds that the Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeds from the Father, and the Western churches later inserted the words and the Son, a phrase that became a lasting point of division between East and West. The dispute concerned both the doctrine of the Spirit's procession and the authority to alter a creed received from an ecumenical council.

We believe in one holy catholic and apostolic church, the creed continues, confessing one baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and looking for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. The closing clauses gather the church, the sacrament, and the final hope into a single act of trust, ending the confession not with doctrine alone but with expectation.

The creed sometimes attributed to Athanasius states the doctrine of the Trinity with unusual rigour, declaring that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and yet there are not three Gods but one God. It insists that the persons are neither confounded nor the substance divided, and it warns that this faith must be held whole and undefiled by anyone who would be saved.

The confessions of the churches were not regarded by their authors as rivals to scripture but as summaries of it, statements of what the church understood the scriptures to teach. They were subscribed by ministers as a public testimony, and the practice of confession served both to instruct the faithful and to mark the boundary between the church's teaching and the errors it judged the scriptures to exclude.

Actions are judged by intentions, and every person will be rewarded according to what he intended. So whoever migrated for the sake of God and his messenger, his migration was for God and his messenger; and whoever migrated to gain some worldly benefit or to marry a woman, his migration was for that which he migrated. This tradition, placed at the head of many collections, makes the inward purpose the measure of every deed.

The science of hadith developed an elaborate apparatus for testing the reliability of reports. Each tradition is preceded by its chain of transmitters, and the scholars examined every name in the chain, asking whether the transmitter was truthful, whether his memory was sound, and whether he could plausibly have met the one from whom he claimed to have heard. A break in the chain or a weakness in a transmitter lowered the grade of the report.

None of you truly believes, the Prophet is reported to have said, until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. The traditions of this kind, brief and ethical, were gathered into collections of forty hadith intended for memorisation, and teachers held that a person who preserved and acted upon such a number would be raised among the learned.

The hadith are graded by the scholars into the sound, the good, and the weak, and within the sound a further distinction is drawn for traditions transmitted by so many independent chains that collusion in error is inconceivable. A ruling in law may be built upon a sound report, while a weak report is admitted, if at all, only for the encouragement of virtuous deeds and never as a basis for obligation.

The Prophet said that religion is sincerity, and when his companions asked, to whom, he answered, to God, to his book, to his messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims, and to the common people. The tradition is brief, yet the commentators have written at length upon it, finding in its few words a whole account of the obligations of faith toward God, scripture, the Prophet, and the community.

A category of tradition known as the sacred hadith records words attributed to God himself, conveyed through the Prophet but not part of the Quran. In one such report God says that he is as his servant thinks he is, and that he is with the servant when the servant remembers him. These traditions are distinguished from the Quran in that their wording is the Prophet's, while their meaning is from God.

The companion who reported the largest number of traditions explained that he had remained in the company of the Prophet while others were occupied with trade and farming, and that he had prayed for a memory that would not lose what it received. The scholars of hadith recorded such accounts to establish how a transmitter came by his knowledge and why his reports might be trusted.

The compilers of the great collections did not gather every report they encountered. One scholar is said to have examined hundreds of thousands of traditions and to have admitted only a few thousand into his book, performing a ritual prayer for guidance before recording each one. The collections that survived this winnowing came to be regarded by the community as the most reliable record of the Prophet's words and conduct.

When a tradition appeared to contradict the Quran or another well-established report, the scholars sought to reconcile the two, to determine which was later and so abrogating, or to judge one of them defective in transmission. The discipline of resolving such conflicts became a branch of learning in its own right, for the jurist could not act on a report whose standing relative to other sources was unsettled.

The Prophet is reported to have said that whoever attributes to him a saying he did not utter should prepare a seat for himself in the fire. This warning, itself a hadith, made the fabrication of traditions a grave offence and gave urgency to the work of the critics, who held that the integrity of the prophetic record was a trust the community was bound to guard.

The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction. The book of Proverbs opens by naming reverence as the root from which all true understanding grows, and the sayings that follow contrast the wise and the foolish, the diligent and the sluggard, the one who guards his tongue and the one whose words bring ruin.

Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The book of Ecclesiastes presses the question of meaning to its limit, surveying labour, pleasure, and wisdom alike and finding each unable to secure a lasting gain.

For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted; a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance. The Preacher arranges the contraries of human life in pairs, observing the rhythm of times that no one can hasten or hold back.

The book of Job sets the suffering of a righteous man against the easy doctrine of his friends, who insist that affliction must be the wage of sin. From the whirlwind God answers Job not with an explanation but with a series of questions about the foundations of the earth and the wildness of creation, and Job, having spoken of things too wonderful for him, lays his hand upon his mouth.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths. The proverb sets a posture of dependence against the self-sufficiency that the wisdom tradition counts a form of folly, and it promises not the absence of difficulty but a path made straight for the one who walks in reverence.

Wisdom in the book of Proverbs is personified as a woman who cries aloud in the street and calls at the city gates, offering her instruction to all who will receive it. She declares that the Lord possessed her at the beginning of his work, that she was beside him as a master craftsman when he established the heavens, and that whoever finds her finds life.

A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly. Many of the proverbs concern the power of speech, observing that words can heal or wound, that a fitly spoken word is like apples of gold, and that even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise.

The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. So Ecclesiastes closes, gathering its long meditation on the emptiness of human striving into a final counsel. Some interpreters read the ending as a later editor's resolution, others as the Preacher's own settled conclusion, but it stands as the book's last word on how a life is to be lived under the sun.

The wisdom literature speaks across the cultures of the ancient world, and Israel's sages drew upon a wider tradition while turning it toward the fear of the Lord. The book of Proverbs even incorporates a section of sayings of the wise that resembles Egyptian instruction, yet the whole is governed by the conviction that wisdom is not mere shrewdness but a way of life ordered toward the will of the creator.

Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest. The proverb sends the idle to learn from the small creatures, and the wisdom tradition often draws its lessons from the close observation of nature, finding in the conies and the locusts examples of an order that the careless human heart ignores.

The Quran tells the story of Joseph, calling it the most beautiful of narratives. The boy is cast into the well by his brothers, sold for a paltry price, tried in the house of the Egyptian, and imprisoned though innocent, until at last he is raised to authority and his brothers come before him not knowing him. When he reveals himself he does not reproach them but says that God has been gracious, for he keeps account of patient endurance.

When Moses came to the burning bush, the Quran relates, he was called by name and told to remove his sandals, for he stood in a sacred valley. He was shown the sign of the staff that became a serpent and the hand that shone white, and he was sent to a tyrant with the request that he loosen his tongue so that the people might understand his speech. The narrative dwells on the prophet's fear and his prayer for a helper.

Abraham is presented in the Quran as the friend of God who broke with the idols of his people. He questioned the worship of the stars and the sun and the moon, observing that what set could not be his Lord, and he confronted his father and his community, asking what they worshipped and whether the carved images could hear them or do them good or harm. The narrative makes him the model of pure devotion to the one God.

The Quran recounts the trial of Abraham, who saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son, and who told the boy of the vision. The son answered that his father should do as he was commanded and would find him, God willing, among the patient. When both had submitted and the father had laid the son down, a voice called out that he had fulfilled the dream, and a great sacrifice was given in the boy's place.

The Quran tells of Noah, who called his people for many years and was met with mockery, and who built the ark while they passed by and laughed. The flood came at the appointed sign, and the Quran adds the detail that one of Noah's own sons refused the call, trusting in a mountain to save him from the water, and was overtaken among the drowned, so that the prophet learned that kinship does not avail against unbelief.

The story of Mary in the Quran tells how she withdrew from her people and how the angel announced to her a pure son, and she asked how she could have a son when no man had touched her. The infant Jesus, the Quran relates, spoke from the cradle in her defence, declaring himself a servant of God to whom the scripture had been given and the prophethood appointed.

The Quran narrates the encounter of Moses with a servant of God who possessed a knowledge given from the divine presence. Moses asked to follow him and was warned that he would not be able to bear it patiently, and when the companion damaged a boat, slew a youth, and repaired a wall for no wage, Moses protested each time, until the meaning of each act was disclosed and Moses understood that hidden wisdom may wear the appearance of wrong.

The Quran recounts the contest of Moses with the magicians of the tyrant, who cast down their ropes and staffs so that they seemed to move by their enchantment. Moses cast down his staff, and it swallowed what they had falsely made, and the magicians, recognising a power beyond their craft, fell down in prostration and declared their belief in the Lord of Moses and Aaron, though the tyrant threatened them.

The narratives of the earlier prophets are told in the Quran not as bare history but as admonition, and the recital frequently pauses to draw the lesson, declaring that in their stories there is a sign for those who possess understanding. The prophets are presented as a single succession bearing the same message, and the people of each age are warned by the fate of those who rejected the messengers before them.

The Quran tells of Jonah, who departed in anger and was swallowed by the great fish, and who called out from the darkness that there is no god but the one God, that he was glorified, and that the one who called had been among the wrongdoers. The Quran declares that had he not been among those who glorify God, he would have remained in the belly of the fish until the day of resurrection.

The classical tradition affirms that God is simple, that there is in God no composition of parts, no distinction of substance and accident, no real difference between the divine essence and its existence. Whatever is said of God is said of the one undivided reality, so that the divine wisdom and the divine power and the divine goodness are not separate perfections added to the essence but the one essence considered under different names.

To speak of God's eternity is not to speak of an endless duration but of a mode of being that has no succession, in which there is no before and no after. The whole of the divine life is possessed at once, and the theologians have described eternity as the complete and simultaneous possession of unbounded life, contrasting it with time, which is the measure of motion and change.

The doctrine of divine immutability holds that God does not change, neither acquiring new perfections nor losing any, for change would imply a passage from potency to act, and in God there is no unrealised potential. The scriptures that speak of God repenting or relenting are read by this tradition as accommodations to human understanding, describing the constancy of the divine will under the appearance of a change.

The way of negation in theology proceeds by denying of God every limitation found in creatures, so that God is called infinite, incomprehensible, and ineffable. By this path the mind does not grasp what God is but learns ever more exactly what God is not, and the theologians who walked this way held that the highest knowledge of God in this life is to know that God exceeds all that we can know.

When the same name is given to God and to a creature, the theologians ask whether it is used in the same sense, in entirely different senses, or in a third way. They answer that it is neither univocal nor merely equivocal but analogical, for the goodness of a creature is a true likeness of the divine goodness while falling infinitely short of it, so that the word carries a real but proportioned meaning.

Divine omniscience is held to extend not only to all actual things but to all possible things and to the free acts of creatures, and the theologians have long debated how this knowledge is compatible with freedom. Some have located the answer in the eternity of God, who sees all times at once as present, so that the divine knowledge does not foresee the free act as future but beholds it as it occurs.

The attribute of omnipresence is explained by the tradition not as the spreading of a vast body through space but as the presence of the divine power and knowledge and essence to every place and every thing. God is in all things, the theologians say, as the cause is present to its effect, sustaining each creature in being, and there is no place from which God is absent because there is no being that does not depend on him.

The Islamic theologians debated whether the attributes of God, his knowledge, his power, his speech, are identical with the essence or in some way distinct from it. Some held that the attributes are neither the essence nor other than the essence, a formula meant to affirm their reality while denying any plurality of gods, and the discussion shaped the doctrine of the divine names that the tradition holds to be ninety-nine.

The mercy of God is held by the theologians to be coextensive with his being, and the scriptures of more than one tradition declare that his mercy embraces all things and outstrips his wrath. To speak of divine justice and divine mercy as two attributes in tension is, on this view, to forget the divine simplicity, for the same single act by which God is just is the act by which he is merciful, and the appearance of conflict belongs to the limited human standpoint.

And God said to Noah, this is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. The first of the great covenants is made not with a people but with all flesh, and its sign is given in the sky for every generation to see.

The covenant with Abraham is announced as a promise, that the patriarch will be made into a great nation, that his name will be made great, and that in him all the families of the earth will be blessed. The narrative records the covenant as a binding act, passing between the divided pieces of the sacrifice while a deep sleep falls upon Abraham, so that the obligation is shown to rest upon the divine initiative.

At Sinai the covenant takes the form of a bond between God and the people redeemed from Egypt. You shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, the words declare, and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people answer that all the Lord has spoken they will do, and the covenant is ratified with blood sprinkled upon the altar and upon the assembly.

The covenant with David promises an enduring house, declaring that the king's offspring will be established after him and that his throne will be made firm forever. The prophet brings this word to David in the night, and the covenant becomes the seed of a long expectation, for when the kingdom falls the promise is remembered, and the hope of an anointed heir to David's throne is carried into the prophetic books.

Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant I made with their fathers. I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. The prophet Jeremiah looks beyond the broken covenant to one inscribed not on stone but within.

The covenant at Sinai is structured with elements that scholars have compared to the treaties of the ancient Near East, including a historical preamble recalling the deliverance from Egypt, the stipulations of the law, the provision for the document to be read aloud, and the blessings and curses attached to obedience and disobedience. The form binds the people in gratitude for a rescue already accomplished.

The book of Deuteronomy renews the covenant on the plains of Moab for the generation about to enter the land. Choose life, the people are urged, that you and your offspring may live, loving the Lord your God, obeying his voice, and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days. The covenant is set before them as a decision, with heaven and earth called to witness.

After the exile the covenant is solemnly renewed when the people gather and the law is read aloud, and the leaders set their seal to a written agreement to walk in the law of God. The narrative shows the covenant not as a single event in the past but as a relationship returned to and reaffirmed, broken by the people and yet held open by the faithfulness ascribed to God.

The Sabbath is given as a sign of the covenant, a perpetual reminder set within the rhythm of every week. The Israelites are to keep the Sabbath throughout their generations, the text declares, as a covenant forever, for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested. The covenant is thus woven into the ordering of time itself.

Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was. The mystical writers seized on this verse, finding in the dark cloud upon the mountain a figure of the soul's highest knowledge of God, which is not a flood of light but an entry into a luminous darkness, where the mind, having let go of every image and concept, is united to the one who cannot be seen.

The vision of Isaiah in the temple, in which the prophet sees the Lord high and lifted up and the seraphim crying holy, holy, holy, was read by the contemplative tradition as a pattern of the soul's encounter with the divine majesty. The prophet's cry that he is undone, a man of unclean lips, and the burning coal that touches and purges his mouth, were taken as a figure of the purification that precedes any true ascent.

The ladder that Jacob saw in his dream, set up on the earth with its top reaching to heaven and the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, became in the monastic tradition an image of the spiritual life. One ancient writer composed a treatise of thirty steps, naming the virtues by which the soul climbs from the renunciation of the world toward the love that crowns the ascent.

The apostle writes that he knew a man caught up to the third heaven, whether in the body or out of the body he could not tell, who heard things that cannot be told, which no one may utter. The mystics returned often to this passage, finding in it a warrant for an experience of God so far beyond ordinary cognition that language fails before it, and a reticence that they took as the proper response to such a gift.

The Song of Songs, with its language of seeking and finding, of the bride who rises in the night to look for the one her soul loves, was read by the mystical tradition as the deepest scripture of the soul's union with God. Bernard preached scores of sermons on its opening verses, treating the kiss of the mouth as the longed-for immediacy of contemplative love.

The Sufi tradition read the night journey of the Prophet as the supreme account of mystical ascent, the rising through the heavens to the lote tree of the farthest boundary, beyond which none may pass. The masters of the inner path spoke of their own contemplations as a journey of the heart along the same ascending stations, drawing near to the divine presence and returning to the world transformed.

Elijah at the mountain of God did not find the Lord in the great wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in a sound of sheer silence. The mystics treasured this passage, reading the still small voice as a teaching that the divine presence is met not in the spectacular but in a stillness so deep that the soul must itself fall silent to perceive it.

The chariot that Ezekiel beheld by the river, the wheels within wheels, the living creatures, the gleaming throne above the firmament, became in the Jewish mystical tradition the central object of contemplation. The discipline that grew around this vision was guarded with care, for the sages held that the work of the chariot should not be expounded except to one who is wise and understands of his own knowledge.

The transfiguration on the mountain, where the face of Jesus shone like the sun and his garments became white as light, was read by the contemplative tradition as a glimpse of the glory that the soul is destined to share. The Eastern church in particular found in the uncreated light of the mountain a sign of the divine energies, accessible to those whose hearts have been purified by long prayer.

One mystical writer described the ascent of the soul to God as a movement through three ways, the way of purgation in which the soul is cleansed of its disordered loves, the way of illumination in which it is filled with the light of contemplation, and the way of union in which it is joined to the divine. The scriptures, on this reading, contain at every turn the map of this interior journey.

The Jain scriptures teach the vow of non-harm as the first and greatest of the disciplines, extending it not only to human beings and animals but to the smallest forms of life, the creatures of the water, the earth, and the air. The monk who has taken this vow strains his drinking water, sweeps the path before he steps, and speaks gently, for the scriptures hold that every living being shrinks from injury as he himself does.

The Tattvartha Sutra, the most concise statement of Jain doctrine, opens by declaring that right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct together constitute the path to liberation. The text then unfolds a precise account of the categories of reality, the bondage of the soul by karmic matter, and the gradual stripping away of that matter by austerity, so that the soul, made luminous, rises to the summit of the universe.

The Jain doctrine of the manifold nature of reality teaches that every statement about a thing is true only from a particular standpoint, and that the whole truth exceeds any single assertion. The scriptures illustrate this with the parable of the blind men and the elephant, each describing the part he touches and each mistaken in taking his portion for the whole; wisdom lies in qualifying every claim.

The Gathas, the oldest portion of the Zoroastrian scriptures, are hymns attributed to the prophet Zarathustra himself, and they address the wise Lord in the language of a seeker pressing urgent questions. In them the prophet asks who set the course of the sun and the stars, who upholds the earth and the clouds, and through whom the dawn and noon and night come, declaring that he asks in order to know the maker of all.

The Zoroastrian tradition gathers the moral teaching into a threefold formula that the scriptures repeat as the path of the faithful: good thoughts, good words, and good deeds. The believer is called to align the inner life, the speech, and the action with truth, taking part in the great struggle between truth and falsehood that the scriptures place at the centre of the cosmos.

The Acaranga Sutra, among the oldest of the Jain texts, preserves the discipline of the wandering monk in spare and severe prose. It teaches that the one who knows the nature of harm knows the nature of restraint, and it describes the ascetic who endures heat and cold, hunger and the abuse of others, without complaint, for the scriptures hold that equanimity under hardship purifies the soul of its bondage.

The Zoroastrian scriptures present the wise Lord as the creator of truth and the source of the good mind, and they place over against him the lie and the destructive spirit. The Gathas frame human life as a choice between the two ways, and they teach that each soul, by its thoughts and words and deeds, takes its side in a conflict whose outcome is the renewal of the world.

The Jain scriptures teach a doctrine of many-sidedness in expression, by which every claim is prefixed with a particle meaning in some respect, acknowledging that the same object may be described as existing and as not existing, as permanent and as changing, according to the aspect considered. This discipline of qualified assertion is presented in the texts as the verbal counterpart of the vow of non-harm, a refusal to do violence even in speech.

The Zoroastrian liturgical texts include the Yasna, recited during the central ritual, and the prayers known by their opening words, which the faithful learn to repeat. The most sacred of these short prayers is held to contain in a few words the essence of the religion, and the tradition teaches that its recitation, performed with understanding, drives away the powers of evil.

The Jain texts describe the ladder of spiritual progress as a series of stages through which the soul rises from the deepest delusion to the threshold of liberation. At each stage a portion of the obscuring karma falls away, and at the summit the soul attains omniscience, perceiving all things in all times at once, and at the dissolution of the body it rises, free of all matter, to abide in unbroken bliss.
