Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice say that the dwelling place of God is with man, and that he will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

The apocalyptic vision is characteristically conveyed through symbol, the beast rising from the sea, the dragon, the seals, the trumpets, and the bowls, and the seer is shown rather than told. The book of Daniel narrates a vision of four beasts and of one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, and the symbolism is partly interpreted within the text and partly left for the reader to ponder.

The book of Revelation opens by pronouncing a blessing on the one who reads aloud the words of the prophecy and on those who hear and keep what is written, for the time is near. The seer addresses seven churches with words of commendation and warning, and only then does the vision widen to the throne in heaven, the scroll sealed with seven seals, and the Lamb who is found worthy to open it.

Apocalyptic writing arises in times of crisis and addresses a people under pressure, assuring them that the present distress is known to God and that the powers that oppress them stand under judgment. The genre lifts the reader's eyes from the immediate scene to a cosmic conflict already decided, and its purpose is less prediction than endurance, urging the faithful to hold fast.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life, and the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done. The apocalyptic vision ends not in chaos but in judgment and renewal, and the book of life is presented as the register of those who belong to the city that descends from heaven.

The little apocalypse in the gospels has Jesus foretell the destruction of the temple and the trials that will precede the end, warning the disciples not to be led astray by those who claim the time has come. He tells them that of that day and hour no one knows, not the angels, nor the Son, but only the Father, and he urges watchfulness in the manner of servants awaiting the return of their master.

The numbers of apocalyptic literature carry meaning beyond arithmetic, the seven that signifies completeness, the twelve of the tribes and the apostles, the thousand years, and the number of the beast. Interpreters across the centuries have read these figures variously, some seeking historical referents and others a symbolic theology of fullness and limitation, and the genre invites this layered reading by its very form.

The vision of the dry bones given to Ezekiel shows a valley filled with bones very dry, and the prophet is asked whether they can live. At the word of prophecy the bones come together, bone to its bone, and sinew and flesh come upon them, and the breath enters them, and they stand upon their feet, a vast multitude. The vision is interpreted as the promise that a people counted dead in exile will be raised and brought home.

The Qumran community produced apocalyptic writings that divided humanity into the sons of light and the sons of darkness, and that anticipated a final war in which the forces of righteousness, aided by the angels, would overcome the powers of wickedness. These texts express the conviction common to apocalyptic literature that history is moving toward a decisive confrontation in which God will openly establish his rule.

Behold, the seer hears, I am making all things new. And he is told to write, for these words are trustworthy and true. The book of Revelation closes its vision with the promise of a renewed creation rather than a destroyed one, and the final chapters describe the river of the water of life and the tree whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, so that the apocalypse ends in restoration.

Listen, my son, to the master's instructions, and incline the ear of your heart. The Rule of Benedict opens with this summons, addressing the one who would enter the monastic life as a son to be taught, and it goes on to describe a school for the Lord's service in which nothing harsh and nothing burdensome is to be set down, but in which the heart, as it advances, runs the way of the commandments with delight.

The monastic rule orders the day around the offices of prayer, dividing the hours so that the community gathers to chant the psalms at fixed intervals from before dawn until the close of the night. Nothing, the Rule insists, is to be preferred to the work of God, and the brother who is late for the office is to be corrected, for the discipline of the appointed hours shapes the whole rhythm of the common life.

The vow of obedience binds the monk to receive the command of the superior as if it came from God, and the Rule treats this surrender of the private will as the heart of the conversion of life. Yet it tempers the demand with provision for the brother who finds a command beyond his strength, instructing him to explain his difficulty with patience and not to refuse outright.

Idleness, the Rule declares, is the enemy of the soul, and therefore the brothers should be occupied at certain times in manual labour and at other times in sacred reading. The monastic discipline distributes the day among prayer, work, and study, and it holds that the monk who labours with his hands and reads the scriptures is guarded against the wandering thoughts that beset the unoccupied mind.

The Buddhist monastic code, the Vinaya, sets out the rules by which the community of monks orders its life, and the tradition holds that each rule was laid down by the Buddha in response to a particular occasion of misconduct. The most serious offences entail expulsion from the order, while lesser faults require confession before the assembled community, which gathers on the days of the new and full moon to recite the code in full.

The Rule devotes a long chapter to humility, describing it as a ladder of twelve steps by which the monk ascends, paradoxically, by descent. The first step is the constant remembrance of the fear of God, and the steps that follow lead through obedience, patience under injustice, and the confession of faults, until the monk arrives at a love that casts out fear and does naturally what once was done with effort.

The Rule legislates for the reception of guests, instructing that all who arrive be welcomed as Christ himself, for he will say that he was a stranger and was taken in. The guest is to be met with prayer and the kiss of peace, and proper honour is to be shown especially to the poor and to pilgrims, since in the rich the awe they inspire already secures their welcome.

The early rule attributed to Pachomius organised the monks into houses under the charge of a senior brother, and it regulated the smallest details of dress, meals, and silence, so that the community moved with a common discipline. The aim of such precise legislation was not the multiplication of restrictions but the removal of friction, freeing the monk from the wear of countless small decisions so that the mind might be given to prayer.

The Rule provides for the correction of faults by a graded discipline, beginning with private warning, proceeding to public rebuke, and reaching, for the obstinate, the penalty of separation from the common table and the common prayer. Yet the same Rule charges the superior to seek the wandering brother as a shepherd seeks the lost sheep, and to apply correction as a wise physician applies medicine, with discernment of each soul.

The monastic discipline of silence is not the mere absence of speech but a guarding of the tongue that the rule treats as a positive virtue. The Rule of Benedict permits the brothers to speak rarely, even of good and holy matters, and counsels that the disciple's part is to keep silence and to listen, for in the multitude of words, the scripture warns, sin is not lacking.

The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. The two parables press the same point: the kingdom is worth everything one has.

A sower went out to sow, and as he sowed some seed fell along the path and was devoured, some on rocky ground where it sprang up quickly and withered, some among thorns that choked it, and some on good soil where it bore grain a hundredfold. When his disciples asked the meaning, Jesus explained that the seed is the word and the soils are the hearts that receive it in different ways.

The kingdom of heaven, Jesus said, is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches. The parable sets a hidden and unpromising beginning against an unexpected and sheltering greatness.

The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. One owed an enormous sum he could not pay, and the king, moved with pity, forgave the whole debt. But that servant went out and seized a fellow servant who owed him a trifling amount and had him thrown into prison. The parable of the unforgiving servant ties the mercy received to the mercy required of the one who received it.

The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early to hire labourers for his vineyard, agreeing with them for a denarius a day. He hired others at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the eleventh, and at evening he paid each the same wage. When those hired first grumbled, he answered that he had done them no wrong, and asked whether his generosity should provoke envy.

The kingdom of heaven, the parable runs, is like a net thrown into the sea that gathered fish of every kind. When it was full the fishermen drew it ashore and sorted the good into containers and threw away the bad. So it will be at the close of the age, Jesus said, when the angels will separate the evil from the righteous. The parable, like that of the weeds, defers the sorting to the end.

He told them another parable: the kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened. The image is quiet and domestic, yet the woman has worked a large quantity of dough, and the parable holds together the hiddenness of the kingdom's working with the totality of the change it brings about.

A man planted a vineyard, the parable of the weeds begins, but while everyone slept his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat. When the servants asked whether they should gather the weeds, the master said no, lest in gathering them they uproot the wheat as well; let both grow together until the harvest. The parable counsels patience with a mixed field and reserves the separation to the appointed time.

The kingdom of heaven, Jesus said, may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son and sent his servants to call those who were invited, but they would not come. So he sent his servants into the roads to invite everyone they found, both bad and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests. The parable warns that the first-invited may forfeit their place and that the feast will not remain empty.

The teaching in parables, the gospels note, was itself a deliberate manner of speech, for Jesus said that to those given understanding more would be given, while to others the same parable would remain a riddle. The parable thus both reveals and conceals, opening the kingdom to the one who ponders it and leaving it closed to the one who hears only the surface of the story.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: When Moses asked the name of the one who sent him, the answer given at the bush was a phrase often rendered I am who I am, and the messenger was told to say that I am has sent him. The interpreters have read this name as a declaration of the divine self-existence, of a being that depends on nothing and is bound to no description, and the four letters derived from it became the name treated as too holy to pronounce.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The Islamic tradition holds that God has ninety-nine names, the most beautiful names, and that whoever counts them and grasps their meaning enters the garden. Among them are the Compassionate, the Merciful, the Sovereign, the Holy, the Source of Peace, the Guardian of Faith, the Mighty, the Forgiving. The believer is taught to call upon God by these names, for the Quran instructs that to God belong the most beautiful names and bids the worshipper invoke him by them.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The Hebrew scriptures address God by many titles, the Most High, the Lord of Hosts, the Holy One of Israel, the Rock, the Shepherd, and each name carries a portion of the divine reality into the worshipper's speech. The tradition holds that the name reveals the bearer, and so the multiplication of names is not confusion but a widening confession, each title naming a face that God has turned toward his people.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The scriptures of the Hindu tradition delight in the litany of divine names, and the practice of reciting the thousand names of the deity is held to be a discipline of devotion in its own right. Each name in such a litany is a meditation, naming the divine as the support of the worlds, the abode of all beings, the imperishable, the formless and the all-formed, so that the recitation carries the mind through the whole sweep of the divine being.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The divine name is treated in many scriptures as itself a presence and a power, not a mere label. The psalmist sings that the name of the Lord is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe, and the prophets speak of those who love the name and those who profane it. To act in the name is to act under its authority, and to bear the name is to belong to the one who bears it.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The Sikh scripture opens with the syllable that names the one reality and proceeds to call it the True Name, teaching that the divine is known and remembered through the name above all other practices. The tradition holds that the name was true before the ages, is true now, and shall be true hereafter, and the worshipper is counselled to dwell on it with every breath, for the name is the bridge between the soul and its source.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The negative theology insists that no name fully fits the divine, and yet the scriptures press on naming, for the worshipper must address the one to whom prayer is offered. The tradition resolves the tension by holding that the names are true as far as they go and yet always exceeded, so that to call God good is to speak truly while knowing that the divine goodness surpasses the human meaning of the word.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The gospel of John gathers a series of declarations in which Jesus takes upon his own lips the form of the divine name, saying I am the bread of life, I am the light of the world, I am the good shepherd, I am the resurrection and the life. The interpreters have heard in these sayings an echo of the name revealed at the bush, an identification placed in the mouth of the one who speaks them.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The third commandment forbids taking the name of God in vain, and the tradition has read this prohibition broadly, as a guard against false oaths, against careless speech, and against any use of the name that empties it of reverence. Out of regard for the holiness of the name the later tradition substituted other words in reading aloud, so that the name might be honoured in being not pronounced.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The litany of divine names in the scriptures often pairs attributes that seem opposed, calling God both the one who brings low and the one who lifts up, both the one who wounds and the one who heals, both near and hidden. The tradition takes these pairings not as contradiction but as the only honest way to name a reality that contains within its single simplicity all that is scattered and divided among creatures.

The formation of the Hebrew canon proceeded in stages, with the books of the law receiving authoritative status earliest, the prophets following, and the writings settling last. The tradition records debates among the sages over certain books, whether the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes should be counted among the sacred writings, and the decision to include them reflects a judgment that they too were spoken in the spirit.

The Christian church did not receive its New Testament canon by a single decree but recognised over time which writings the churches had used in worship and found to bear the apostolic witness. Lists drawn up by individual bishops and councils gradually converged, and the criteria applied included apostolic origin, conformity to the rule of faith, and widespread acceptance among the churches.

The Muslim tradition holds that the Quran was collected into a single authoritative codex within the first decades after the Prophet's death. The reciters who had preserved the revelation were consulted, the written fragments were gathered, and a standard text was established and copies sent to the major centres, while variant copies were set aside, so that the community would recite from one text.

Certain early Christian writings, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Epistle of Barnabas, the letter attributed to Clement, were read and valued in some churches but did not finally enter the canon. Their exclusion was not a verdict that they were worthless but a judgment that they did not carry the apostolic authority of the books received, and they continued to be copied and read with respect outside the canon.

The teacher Marcion, in the second century, proposed a drastically reduced canon, rejecting the Hebrew scriptures entirely and keeping only an edited gospel and a selection of Paul's letters. The church's response, in defining a broader canon that held the Old and New Testaments together, was shaped in part by the need to answer his challenge and to affirm the unity of the God of Israel with the God of the gospel.

The books known as the apocrypha or deuterocanonical writings, present in the Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures but absent from the shorter Hebrew collection, have a contested standing among Christian communities. Some churches receive them as fully canonical, others place them in a secondary category useful for instruction, and the difference is one of the lasting markers between the traditions.

The Buddhist tradition does not possess a single closed canon, for the scriptures were preserved in several languages and several collections. The Pali canon, organised into three baskets of discipline, discourses, and higher teaching, is held authoritative by one branch, while other branches received a wider body of sutras, and the question of which texts are the genuine word of the Buddha has been answered differently across the schools.

The canonical lists that survive from the early centuries show a stable core recognised everywhere, the four gospels and the letters of Paul, surrounded by a fringe of books whose standing was settled only gradually, among them the letter to the Hebrews, the book of Revelation, and the shorter general epistles. The process reveals a canon discovered through use rather than imposed by authority.

The Hindu scriptures distinguish between texts regarded as heard, the eternal revelation comprising the Vedas, and texts regarded as remembered, the vast body of tradition including the epics and the law codes. The first category is held to be authorless and beginningless, and the second derives its authority from being grounded in the first, a distinction that orders the immense literature of the tradition.

The recognition of a canon carried with it the conviction that revelation, in some decisive sense, was complete, and that the community would thereafter live by interpreting the received books rather than by adding to them. This belief gave the canon its function as a boundary, a fixed measure against which later teaching could be tested, and the very word for canon means a rule or measuring rod.

Holy God, holy and mighty, holy and immortal, have mercy on us. This ancient invocation, sung in the liturgies of the Eastern church, addresses the divine holiness three times and answers it with a plea for mercy, and the tradition surrounds it with accounts of its origin so that the congregation receives it as a prayer given rather than composed.

Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased. The greater doxology, drawn from the song of the angels at the nativity and expanded by the early church, opens the praise of the liturgy and gathers the worshippers into the heavenly hymn, blessing and adoring and giving thanks before the petition begins.

The prayer of thanksgiving at the table recalls the whole work of salvation before it asks anything, rehearsing the creation, the covenant, and the redemption, so that the petition rests upon remembrance. Lift up your hearts, the celebrant says, and the people answer that they lift them to the Lord, and the dialogue draws the assembly into the act of giving thanks that gives the rite its name.

Praised are you, Lord our God, sovereign of the universe. This formula opens the blessings of the Jewish liturgy, and the worshipper repeats it before bread and wine, before the lighting of lamps, before the study of the law, and on beholding wonders of nature. The blessing turns the ordinary moment into an occasion of acknowledgement, naming the source of every good before it is received.

Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The central declaration of the Jewish liturgy, recited morning and evening, is followed by the command to love the Lord with all the heart, all the soul, and all the might, and to teach these words to the children and to bind them as a sign upon the hand. The prayer is at once a confession of faith and a charge to transmit it.

The collect, a brief prayer that gathers the petitions of the assembly, follows a tight form: an address to God, a clause recalling some attribute or act, a single petition, an aspiration toward the fruit of the petition, and a closing that prays through Christ. The economy of the form allows it to be heard whole, and the church appoints a proper collect for each day so that the prayer is fitted to the season.

Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, have mercy on us; grant us peace. This invocation, sung before the sharing of the bread, draws on the words by which John pointed to Jesus and turns them into a plea, repeated so that the congregation may dwell on the mercy it asks before approaching the table.

The litany sets a long series of petitions before the assembly, each followed by a brief response of the people, so that the prayer becomes a shared work moving steadily through the needs of the church and the world. The form allows the worshippers to carry many concerns to God without haste, and the repeated response, Lord, have mercy, holds the whole litany together.

The Islamic call to prayer, raised five times daily, proclaims that God is greater than all, bears witness that there is no god but the one God and that the Prophet is his messenger, and summons the hearer to prayer and to success. The words, sung from the place of prayer, are themselves a brief creed, and the believer who answers the call repeats the phrases in reply.

The prayer of confession spoken at the opening of worship acknowledges before God what has been done and left undone, and asks for pardon and amendment. The form of the prayer is corporate, the whole congregation speaking together in the first person plural, so that the confession is offered not as a private reckoning but as the common admission of a people who stand together in need of mercy.

The scriptures speak of a resurrection of the dead, and the apostle, pressed on how the dead are raised and with what kind of body, answers with the image of the seed. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. The teaching affirms continuity and transformation together, denying neither the identity of the one raised nor the change that the raising works.

The Quran describes the day of judgment in vivid terms, the trumpet that will be sounded, the earth shaken, the mountains scattered like carded wool, and every soul brought to account. The scales of justice will be set, and not the weight of a mustard seed will be overlooked, for the record of each deed, however small, will be brought forward and read.

The Hindu and Buddhist scriptures set the question of the afterlife within the long cycle of rebirth, in which the soul or the stream of consciousness passes from life to life according to the deeds it has accumulated. Liberation, on this view, is not a better birth but release from the cycle altogether, the cessation of rebirth and the realisation of a freedom no longer subject to coming and going.

The prophet Daniel was told that many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt, and that those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky. This verse, among the clearest statements of resurrection in the Hebrew scriptures, sets the hope of the faithful against the long silence of death.

The gospels record the promise of Jesus that in his Father's house are many rooms, and that he goes to prepare a place, so that where he is, there his disciples may be also. The eschatological hope of the New Testament is centred less on a description of the place than on the presence of the one with whom the faithful will dwell, the seeing of God face to face.

The scriptures speak both of judgment and of mercy when they turn to the last things, and the tradition has held the two together in tension. The believer is warned to take judgment seriously, for deeds have consequences that reach beyond death, and yet the same scriptures sound the hope that the divine mercy is wider than human reckoning, so that the faithful await the end with both reverence and trust.

The Zoroastrian scriptures teach that the soul, after death, crosses a bridge whose width is determined by the deeds of the life just ended, narrow for the wicked and broad for the righteous. Beyond the individual reckoning the tradition looks toward a final renewal, in which the world will be made perfect, the dead raised, and the wise Lord's creation purified of every trace of the lie.

The book of Revelation ends its vision of the last things with the abolition of death itself, declaring that death and the grave are thrown into the lake of fire, and that in the renewed creation death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying nor pain. The eschatology of the New Testament thus reaches its term not in the survival of the soul but in the undoing of death.

The teaching on the intermediate state, the condition of the soul between death and the general resurrection, has occupied theologians who sought to reconcile the scriptures that speak of the dead as sleeping with those that promise the believer an immediate entry into the divine presence. The traditions have answered variously, but all have held that the final hope is bound to the resurrection of the body and the renewal of the whole creation.

The Buddhist teaching on the afterlife is shaped by the doctrine that there is no permanent self to pass from one life to the next, and so the tradition speaks of rebirth rather than the migration of a soul. What continues, the scriptures suggest, is a stream of conditioned arising, like a flame passed from one lamp to another, neither the same nor entirely different, until the conditions that sustain it are exhausted.

Krishna teaches that even the wise act according to their own nature, for all beings follow their nature, and asks what restraint can avail against it. Yet he distinguishes the nature that drives a person from the disordered loves of attachment and aversion that lie in the path of each sense and its object; these are the enemies, and the disciplined soul performs its appointed duty without falling under their sway.

The doctrine of divine impassibility holds that God is not subject to suffering imposed from without, for nothing can act upon the one on whom all things depend. The scriptures that ascribe grief or anger to God are read by this tradition as describing the effects of the divine will upon creatures, or as accommodations to human speech, while the divine life itself is held to be unshakable blessedness.

The covenant theme runs through the whole of the Hebrew scriptures as the framework of the relationship between God and Israel, and the prophets measure the people against its terms. When they denounce the nation they speak as prosecutors in a covenant lawsuit, and when they comfort it they recall the covenant's promises, so that the same bond grounds both the judgment and the hope.

The Sufi commentators read the Quranic verse of light, in which God is named the light of the heavens and the earth, as a description of the inner illumination of the heart. The niche, the lamp, the glass, and the blessed olive tree are taken as figures of the stages by which the divine light is kindled in the purified soul, and the saying that it is light upon light is read as the meeting of the light of revelation with the light of native faith.

Where the Quran speaks of the struggle in the path of God, the Sufi exegetes distinguished the lesser struggle against outward enemies from the greater struggle against the lower self. The verse that commands striving with one's wealth and one's soul is read inwardly, the soul becoming the field of the deeper warfare, and the commentary turns a text of conflict into a manual of self-purification.

The Sufi reading of the verse that declares God nearer to a person than the jugular vein finds in it the foundation of the contemplative path. The nearness is not spatial, the commentators teach, but the presence of the divine to the very ground of the self, so that the seeker who travels far in search of God is shown to be seeking what was never absent, and the journey ends in the recognition of an original intimacy.

The covenant of the primordial day, in which the Quran relates that God drew forth the descendants of Adam and asked whether he was not their Lord, and they answered yes, became for the Sufi commentators the charter of the soul's longing. Every later yearning for God, they taught, is the memory of that answer, and the recitation of the verse stirs in the heart a recognition older than the present life.

The Quranic command to remember God much and to glorify him morning and evening was read by the Sufi tradition as the warrant for the discipline of recollection, the repeated invocation of the divine name. The commentators held that the verse describes not an occasional act but a continuous orientation, and that the heart trained by such remembrance comes to recite the name without effort, as the body breathes.

The verse declaring that wherever you turn, there is the face of God was a favourite of the mystical commentators, who read it as a teaching that the divine presence is not confined to any direction or shrine. The heart that has been opened, they taught, beholds the divine countenance in every quarter, and the outward turning toward the place of prayer is the sign of an inward turning that knows no fixed boundary.

The Sufi commentators dwelt on the Quranic account of the meeting of the soul with its Lord, finding in the address to the soul at peace, told to return to its Lord well-pleased and well-pleasing, a description of the journey's end. The soul that has been refined through trial, they taught, attains a tranquillity that is not the absence of feeling but the rest of a desire that has found its object.

The story of Moses asking to behold God, and being told that he would not see him but should look to the mountain, was read by the Sufi exegetes as a teaching on the limits of vision and the necessity of annihilation. When the mountain crumbled and Moses fell senseless, the commentators saw the passing away of the self that must precede any true beholding, and the recovery as the subsistence granted afterward.

The Quranic verses on patience were gathered by the Sufi commentators into a teaching on the stations of the soul, for patience is named the companion of the steadfast and the bringer of a reward beyond reckoning. The commentary distinguished the patience that endures affliction, the patience that holds back from the forbidden, and the patience that perseveres in obedience, treating each as a discipline on the path.

The opening of the chapter named for the early dawn, in which God swears by the morning brightness and the night when it is still, and assures the Prophet that his Lord has not forsaken him, was read by the Sufi commentators as a consolation for the soul in the dark season of withdrawal. The night of the verse becomes the contraction of the heart, and the promised dawn the return of the divine nearness after a season of absence.

I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me. The first words of the Decalogue ground the commandments in an act of deliverance, so that the law is given not to a people newly enslaved but to one already redeemed, and obedience is asked as the response of gratitude rather than the price of freedom.

Honour your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the Lord your God is giving you. The commentators have noted that this commandment, standing between the duties toward God and the duties toward the neighbour, is the only one of the ten that carries a promise, and they have read the honour due to parents as the first form of the reverence that society depends upon.

Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labour and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. The commandment is grounded in two ways across the scriptures, in the rest of God after the work of creation and in the deliverance from bondage, and the tradition has read both groundings together, finding the Sabbath both a remembrance of creation and a charter of rest for the servant and the stranger.

You shall not covet your neighbour's house; you shall not covet your neighbour's wife, nor anything that is your neighbour's. The final commandment differs from the others in reaching beyond the deed to the desire, and the interpreters have found in it a recognition that the outward acts forbidden by the earlier commandments have their root in a craving of the heart that the law also addresses.

The tradition has divided the ten commandments into two tables, the first concerning the duties owed to God and the second the duties owed to the neighbour. When Jesus was asked for the greatest commandment, he named the love of God with all the heart and the love of the neighbour as oneself, and the church has read his answer as the summary of the two tables, the whole law hanging upon these two.

You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour. The commandment, set in the first instance against perjury in a court, has been read by the tradition more broadly as a guard upon truthful speech, forbidding slander, the spreading of rumour, and the silence that lets a falsehood stand. The neighbour's good name, the interpreters teach, is entrusted to the keeping of all who speak of him.

You shall not make for yourself a carved image, the second commandment declares, nor any likeness of anything in heaven above or in the earth beneath. The prohibition has been understood as a guard of the divine transcendence, for an image confines the worshipper's thought of God to a form, and the traditions have differed over how far the commandment extends to all religious imagery and how far it forbids only the worship of idols.

You shall not murder. The commandment, brief and absolute, has occasioned long reflection on the value the scriptures place on human life, made, the tradition holds, in the image of God. The interpreters have asked how the prohibition relates to the taking of life in war and in the execution of justice, and they have drawn from the single clause both a restraint upon violence and a charge to defend the life of the vulnerable.

The Decalogue is given twice in the Hebrew scriptures, once in the account of the giving of the law at the mountain and once in the renewal of the covenant on the plains of Moab, and the two versions differ in small ways, most notably in the grounding of the Sabbath commandment. The tradition has treasured both forms, reading the variation not as a flaw but as a deepening, the same law spoken to two generations.

You shall not steal. The commandment protects the neighbour's property, and the interpreters have extended it to forbid not only theft by stealth but fraud, the withholding of wages, the use of false weights, and every gain taken at the expense of another's right. The tradition reads the commandment as a charge to deal honestly, so that the eighth word becomes the foundation of a just commerce.

Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling near a certain town, and he addressed the monks, saying that there are these two extremes which one who has gone forth should not pursue, the pursuit of sensual pleasure and the pursuit of self-mortification. Avoiding both, the discourse continues, the one who has gone forth has discovered the middle way, which gives rise to vision and to knowledge and leads to peace.

The discourse on the foundations of mindfulness instructs the practitioner to dwell contemplating the body in the body, the feelings in the feelings, the mind in the mind, and the mental objects in the mental objects, ardent and clearly comprehending. This, the Buddha declares, is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, and for the realisation of liberation.

All conditioned things are impermanent, the discourse teaches; when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. All conditioned things are unsatisfactory; when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. All things are without self; when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path of purification, the verses conclude.

The Buddha, in the discourse to the Kalamas, told them not to accept a teaching merely because it is handed down by tradition, or because it is found in scripture, or because it accords with reason, or out of respect for a teacher. When you know for yourselves, he said, that these things are wholesome and blameless and praised by the wise, and when undertaken lead to welfare and happiness, then you should enter upon them.

In the discourse on loving-kindness the practitioner is instructed to radiate a boundless heart toward all beings, above, below, and across, without obstruction, without hatred, without enmity. Just as a mother would protect with her life her only child, so should one cultivate a limitless heart toward all living beings, and this, the discourse declares, is called the sublime abiding.

The Dhammapada opens with the teaching that the mind is the forerunner of all states, that they are wrought by the mind and made of the mind. If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows as the wheel follows the foot of the ox; if one speaks or acts with a serene mind, happiness follows like a shadow that never departs.

The Buddha set forth the four noble truths in his first discourse, declaring that there is suffering, that there is an origin of suffering in craving, that there is the cessation of suffering, and that there is a path leading to the cessation. The path, he taught, has eight factors, right view and right intention, right speech and right action and right livelihood, right effort and right mindfulness and right concentration.

Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world; by non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is an eternal law. So the Dhammapada teaches, and the verse continues that the others do not know that here we must all come to an end, but those who know this still their quarrels at once. The discourse places the cessation of conflict in the recognition of a shared mortality.

In a discourse on the simile of the raft the Buddha compared the teaching to a raft built for crossing a flood. When the traveller has crossed and stands on the far shore, he does not lift the raft onto his head and carry it about; he leaves it and goes on his way. So too, the Buddha said, when you understand the simile of the raft, you should let go even of good states, and much more so of bad ones.

Among the last words of the Buddha recorded in the discourse on the great passing away is the exhortation that all conditioned things are subject to decay, and that the disciples should strive on with diligence. The discourse relates that he had told them the teaching openly, withholding nothing in the closed fist of a teacher, and that they should henceforth be islands unto themselves, with the teaching as their refuge.

In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters. And God said, let there be light, and there was light. The first chapter unfolds the work of creation in a measured sequence of days, each closing with the refrain that God saw it was good.

Then God said, let us make man in our image, after our likeness. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them. The crowning of the creation week with the making of humanity in the divine image has been read across the tradition as the ground of human dignity and of the vocation to rule the earth as a steward rather than a despot.

The second account of creation, beginning with the man formed from the dust of the ground and the breath of life breathed into his nostrils, has a different texture from the first. It moves from a dry land awaiting rain to a planted garden, and it places the human creature at the centre from the start, naming the animals and finding among them no helper fit for him until the woman is made.

And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy. The creation narrative reaches its term not in a final act of making but in a rest, and the tradition has found in this seventh day the pattern of the Sabbath and a hint that the creation is ordered toward a fulfilment beyond mere labour.

The interpreters have long pondered why the scriptures open with two creation accounts that differ in order and emphasis, the first placing the human creature last and the second placing him first. The traditional reading holds that the two are complementary rather than contradictory, the first surveying the cosmic order and the second drawing near to the human story that the rest of the book will tell.

The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. The creation narrative gives the human creature a charge from the beginning, and the words for working and keeping have been read as a teaching that labour is not a curse but a vocation set before the fall, the cultivation of the world being part of the original blessing.

The creation narrative presents the making of the world as an act of speech, for God says and it is so, and the tradition has dwelt on this, finding in the creative word a teaching that the world is intelligible because it is uttered, the expression of a wisdom rather than the residue of a blind necessity. The same divine word, the later scriptures suggest, sustains what it has called into being.

The lights set in the firmament are appointed, the narrative says, to separate the day from the night, to be for signs and for seasons and for days and years. The interpreters have noted that the sun and moon are not named in the account but called simply the greater light and the lesser light, and they have read this reticence as a deliberate refusal to honour with names the bodies that the neighbouring peoples worshipped.

And God blessed them, the narrative says of the living creatures of the sea and the air, telling them to be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters and the earth. The blessing pronounced over the creatures before the making of humanity has been read as a sign that the divine favour rests on the whole order of life, and that the fruitfulness of the world is itself a gift and not a mere fact.

These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created. The narrative uses the same formula of generations that elsewhere in the book introduces the descendants of a family, and the interpreters have read this as a teaching that the cosmos has a history, that it is not a static order but the beginning of a story that the scriptures will carry forward.

The book of Leviticus sets out the law of the sin offering, by which the worshipper who has transgressed unintentionally brings an animal without blemish, lays a hand upon its head, and the blood is applied to the altar so that the priest makes atonement and the sin is forgiven. The laying on of the hand has been read as an act of identification, the worshipper transferring his fault to the offering that stands in his place.

On the day of atonement the high priest is commanded to take two goats, to cast lots upon them, and to send one into the wilderness bearing the iniquities of the people while the other is offered. He confesses over the head of the live goat all the sins of the assembly, and the goat is led away into a solitary land, carrying the burden far from the camp.

Without the shedding of blood, the letter to the Hebrews declares, there is no forgiveness. The epistle reads the whole apparatus of the older sacrifices as a shadow of the good things to come, arguing that the blood of bulls and goats could not finally take away sins but pointed forward to a single offering, after which the worshipper is perfected and the repeated sacrifice is no longer required.

The burnt offering differed from the sin offering in that the whole animal was consumed upon the altar, none of it eaten, and the law describes it as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. The interpreters have read the burnt offering as an act of total self-dedication, the worshipper giving the whole gift to God rather than reserving a portion, so that the rite expressed devotion rather than the bare removal of guilt.

The peace offering, also called the offering of well-being, was unique in that the worshipper shared in eating it, a portion given to God upon the altar, a portion to the priests, and the remainder eaten by the offerer and his household. The rite has been read as a meal of communion, the participants drawn into fellowship with God and with one another at a table whose centre was the altar.

The prophets repeatedly warned that the ritual of sacrifice, performed without justice and mercy, was an offence rather than a service. I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, one prophet declares in the name of God, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. The tradition has held this prophetic word and the priestly law together, reading the ritual as the appointed form of a devotion that must be inward and ethical to be true.

The Passover sacrifice stood apart from the offerings of the temple, a lamb killed by each household and its blood placed on the doorposts, recalling the night of deliverance from Egypt when the destroyer passed over the marked houses. The rite bound the household to the founding act of the nation, and the meal eaten in haste was a yearly re-entry into the story of redemption.

The fourth song of the suffering servant describes one who was wounded for the transgressions of others, upon whom was laid the iniquity of all, and who, like a lamb led to the slaughter, opened not his mouth. The passage transfers the language of sacrifice to a person, and the interpreters of more than one tradition have read it as the meeting point of the ritual of atonement with the figure who bears the burden of the many.

The Vedic scriptures place the sacrifice at the centre of the cosmic order, and the hymn of the cosmic person describes the world itself as fashioned from the offering of a primal being. The ritual fire, fed with the prescribed oblations and accompanied by the appointed verses, was held to sustain the order of the seasons and the gods, so that the sacrifice was understood as a participation in the maintenance of the world.

The grain offering, presented without blood, consisted of fine flour with oil and frankincense, a portion burned upon the altar and the rest given to the priests. The law forbade leaven and honey in what was burned and required salt, called the salt of the covenant. The interpreters have read the grain offering as the gift of the fruit of human labour, the worshipper presenting not a life but the substance by which life is sustained.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: Augustine argued against the Pelagians that the human will, wounded by the fall, cannot turn toward the good without the prior gift of divine grace. The will is free, he held, but its freedom is bent, and grace does not destroy the will but heals it, so that the person delivered comes to choose freely what before he could not even desire. The dispute set the terms for centuries of theological reflection on the relation of grace and freedom.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The scriptures hold together in tension the assertion that salvation is the work of God and the call to the human will to repent and believe. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, the apostle writes, and in the same breath adds that it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. The theologians have read this verse as a charter for affirming both the divine initiative and the human response.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The doctrine of predestination, drawn from the scriptures that speak of God choosing his people before the foundation of the world, has divided the theological traditions. Some have held that God's eternal choice precedes and grounds every human response, while others have insisted that the divine election takes account of the foreseen faith of the believer, and the debate has turned on how to honour both the freedom of grace and the seriousness of the human will.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The medieval theologians distinguished the grace that goes before, awakening the will and disposing it toward the good, from the grace that follows, cooperating with the will once it has been moved. The first they called prevenient, the second cooperating, and the distinction allowed them to teach that the whole movement of conversion is from grace while still affirming that the will, once healed, truly acts.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The Hindu schools of devotion debated a parallel question under the images of the cat and the monkey. In the way of the cat the kitten is carried by its mother and does nothing, the soul wholly passive in the hands of grace; in the way of the monkey the young one clings to its mother, the soul making its own small effort while the divine power sustains it. The two schools framed the relation of grace and effort in these figures.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The Council that addressed the long dispute after Augustine affirmed that the beginning of faith itself, the first stirring of the will toward God, is the gift of grace and not the achievement of unaided nature. Yet the same teaching rejected the harsher conclusion that God predestines any soul to evil, holding that the divine will to save is genuine and that the loss of the lost is to be ascribed to their own resistance.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The Islamic theologians debated whether human acts are created by God or by the human agent, and whether the believer's faith is his own or the gift of God. One school stressed the absolute power of God, holding that he creates the act and the agent merely acquires it; another stressed human responsibility, fearing that to deny it would make the divine judgment unjust. The mainstream tradition sought a middle position that preserved both.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? The apostle's question became a cornerstone of the doctrine of grace, for the theologians read it as ruling out every claim of merit, and as teaching that even the faith by which a person receives salvation is itself a gift, so that gratitude rather than boasting is the only fitting response.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The tradition has distinguished the grace that justifies, by which the sinner is accepted, from the grace that sanctifies, by which the believer is progressively renewed. The first is received at once, the theologians teach, and the second unfolds over the whole of a life, and the two are held together so that the assurance of acceptance does not breed complacency but rather frees the will for the long work of growth in holiness.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The mystery of grace and freedom resists every neat resolution, and the wisest of the theologians have confessed as much. They have held that the scriptures require both affirmations, that nothing good is done without grace and that the human will truly acts, and that the precise manner of their union lies beyond the reach of definition, to be held in faith rather than dissolved by a system.

The Quran establishes the pilgrimage to the sacred house as a duty upon those who are able to make the journey, and it traces the rite to Abraham, who is said to have raised the foundations of the house and to have been commanded to proclaim the pilgrimage among the people. The pilgrim, entering the state of consecration, sets aside the ordinary garments and the ordinary concerns and turns wholly toward the rite.

The songs of ascent in the Psalter were sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the appointed feasts. I was glad when they said to me, let us go to the house of the Lord, one of them begins, and another lifts the traveller's eyes to the hills, asking whence help will come. The collection gives voice to the joy, the longing, and the trust of those on the road to the holy city.

The law of Israel commanded that three times in the year all the males should appear before the Lord at the place he would choose, at the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks, and the feast of booths. The pilgrim festivals gathered the scattered households into a single assembly, and the scriptures bind them to the agricultural year and to the remembered acts of deliverance.

The Quranic account of the pilgrimage describes the running between the two hills, a rite the tradition connects with the search of Hagar for water for her son, and the standing on the plain of Arafat, where the pilgrims gather in supplication. The rites rehearse the story of Abraham and his household, so that the pilgrim walks bodily through a remembered history.

The Hindu scriptures praise the crossing places, the sacred fords where rivers and shrines allow the pilgrim to pass from the ordinary world toward the divine. To bathe at the confluence of the rivers, to circumambulate a holy mountain, to visit the sites of a deity's appearing, is held to cleanse and to bless, and the texts that catalogue these places make the whole land a map of sanctity.

Blessed are those whose strength is in you, the psalm declares, in whose heart are the highways to Zion. As they go through the valley of weeping they make it a place of springs, and they go from strength to strength. The pilgrim psalm reads the journey itself as a transformation, the dry valley made fruitful by those who pass through it with their faces set toward the house of God.

The Buddhist tradition records that the Buddha named four places that a devout person should visit with reverence, the site of his birth, the site of his enlightenment, the site of his first teaching, and the site of his passing away. The pilgrimage to these places, the discourse suggests, stirs in the heart the recollection of the one who taught the path, and the pilgrim who dies on such a journey is said to fare well.

The scriptures often turn the outward pilgrimage into a figure of the inward journey of the soul toward God. The whole life of the faithful is described as a sojourn, a passing through a land that is not the final home, and the patriarchs are praised as those who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, seeking a country of their own.

The farewell sermon delivered by the Prophet on the pilgrimage is preserved in the tradition as a summary of his teaching, addressed to the great assembly gathered on the plain. He spoke of the sanctity of life and property, of the rights of women, of the abolition of the old feuds, and he asked the people whether he had delivered the message, and they answered that he had.

The pilgrim feast of booths commanded the people to dwell for seven days in temporary shelters, that their generations might know that the Lord made the people of Israel dwell in booths when he brought them out of Egypt. The rite carried the pilgrim back into the wilderness wandering, and the fragile shelter became a yearly reminder that security rests not in settled walls but in the keeping of God.

The midrash on the binding of Isaac fills the silences of the terse biblical narrative, asking what passed between father and son on the three days of the journey, and what Abraham felt as he raised the knife. The rabbis multiply readings, some imagining the son a willing participant who asked to be bound tightly lest he flinch, and the midrash thus draws out of a few verses a meditation on faith and obedience.

The rabbis taught that the Torah has seventy faces, meaning that a single verse yields many true interpretations, and they delighted in finding in the smallest features of the text, an unusual spelling, a repeated word, a particle that seems superfluous, an opening for instruction. Nothing in the scripture, they held, is without purpose, and the diligent reader is rewarded with meanings hidden in the letters.

A midrash relates that when God was about to create the human being, the ministering angels divided into parties, some urging the creation because the human would do acts of kindness and truth, and others opposing it because the human would be full of falsehood and strife. While they disputed, the midrash says, God created the human being and said to the angels that the deed was already done.

The midrashic reading often connects a verse from one part of the scripture with a distant verse from another, drawing them together by a shared word so that each illumines the other. This technique treats the whole of the scripture as a single fabric, and the rabbis held that a verse in the law might be unlocked by a phrase in the psalms, since one author, in their belief, had woven the whole.

On the verse that God created the great sea creatures, a midrash records the saying that this refers to the leviathan and its mate, and it weaves a tale of the taming of these creatures lest they overrun the world. The rabbis used such expansions not as mere fancy but to convey teachings about divine providence and the order set upon the powers of chaos.

The rabbis read the verse that Moses went up to God as an occasion to imagine the prophet ascending to the heavenly court, where the angels objected that the precious Torah should not be given to a creature of flesh and blood. Moses, the midrash relates, answered their objections by asking whether the angels had gone down to Egypt or were tempted by idols, and so won the Torah for the people below.

The midrash distinguishes the legal exposition that derives rules from the verses from the narrative and homiletical exposition that draws moral and devotional lessons. The second kind ranges freely, telling stories, posing parables, and ascribing speeches to the figures of the scripture, and the rabbis valued it as the means by which the heart, and not only the mind, is instructed by the text.

A well-known midrash on the verse that proclaims liberty throughout the land asks why the law of the jubilee is placed where it is, and answers with a parable about a debt forgiven and a slave set free, drawing from the legal provision a teaching about the divine ownership of the land and the people. The midrash characteristically turns a statute into an occasion for reflection on the relationship it presupposes.

The rabbis taught that the words of the Torah are like fire and water, freely available to all who thirst, and they explained why the law was given in the wilderness, a place belonging to no one, so that no tribe could claim it as a private possession. The midrash on the giving of the law makes the desert itself a lesson, the open and ownerless ground a sign that the teaching is offered to whoever will receive it.

A midrash on the creation of the first human being teaches that God formed the dust from every quarter of the earth, from the east and the west, the north and the south, so that no place could say that the human being did not belong to it. The rabbis drew from this the lesson that all people share a common ancestry, and that no one may claim a nobler origin than another.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not anything made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The opening of the gospel sets the figure of Jesus within the eternal life of God and the work of creation before it tells a single event of his earthly story.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. The gospel's prologue moves from the eternal Word to the incarnation in a single sentence, and the verb rendered dwelt has been read as an echo of the tabernacle, the Word pitching his tent among a people as the divine presence once filled the sanctuary.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: The gospel records a series of declarations in which Jesus joins the divine name to an image, saying that he is the bread of life, the light of the world, the door of the sheep, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, and the true vine. The interpreters have heard in the form of these sayings the name revealed at the burning bush, taken upon the lips of the one who utters them.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: Before Abraham was, Jesus says in the gospel, I am. The hearers take up stones, understanding the words as a claim that could not be made by a creature, and the gospel records the saying as one of the sharpest expressions of its Christology, the bare verb of being set against the long ages of the patriarch, an assertion of existence that knows no beginning.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: The gospel reaches its term in the confession of the disciple who, beholding the risen one, says my Lord and my God. The interpreters have noted that the gospel opens by declaring the Word to be God and closes with a human being addressing the risen Jesus by the same name, so that the whole narrative is framed by the affirmation of his divinity, the prologue and the confession answering each other.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: I and the Father are one, Jesus declares in the gospel, and elsewhere he says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, that he is in the Father and the Father in him. The gospel presses a unity of the Son with the Father that the later church would seek to articulate in the language of one substance, and the discourses of the gospel furnish much of the scriptural ground for that doctrine.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: The gospel describes the works of Jesus as signs, and after each sign a discourse unfolds its meaning, so that the feeding of the multitude opens into the teaching on the bread of life, and the raising of Lazarus into the saying that he is the resurrection and the life. The miracle, in this gospel, is never told for wonder alone but as a door into the truth of who the worker is.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: The Word that was with God, the gospel teaches, was the light that enlightens everyone, coming into the world. The interpreters have read this verse as a teaching that the eternal Word is the source of all true illumination, present in some manner to every human being, so that the incarnation does not begin the divine self-communication but brings to a focus a light that had never been wholly absent.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: In the long discourse before his death, Jesus prays that his disciples may be one as he and the Father are one, and that the glory given to him may be given to them. The gospel's Christology here opens outward, for the union of the Son with the Father becomes the pattern and the source of the union of the disciples with one another, and the indwelling extends from the Word to those who believe.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: No one has ever seen God; the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known. The closing verse of the prologue states the gospel's understanding of revelation, that the unseen God is disclosed in the Son, who shares the divine life and so can render it known. The whole gospel that follows is offered as that making known, the showing of the Father in the words and works of the Son.

The poet-saint sings that he is a small bird and the divine name his only nest, that he has no learning and no merit, only a longing that will not be stilled. The bhakti hymns set aside the apparatus of ritual and learning and offer instead the bare cry of the heart, declaring that the lord receives the lowly devotee who comes with empty hands and a full love.

Mirabai sings that she has taken the dark lord for her husband and will have no other, that she has danced before the world and let her good name fall, for the love of the divine has made her careless of what people say. The devotional verse of the bhakti poets often speaks in the voice of the beloved, casting the soul's longing for God in the language of an all-consuming human love.

The weaver Kabir sings that the lord is not in the temple nor in the mosque, not in the pilgrimage nor in the fasting, but is found in the breath of the one who seeks, nearer than the seeker's own hands and feet. His verses chide both the priest and the ascetic and call the listener to a simple, inward devotion that needs no outward sign.

The poet declares that he has no other refuge, that he has tried the ways of knowledge and of works and found them dry, and that he flings himself at the feet of the lord as a child runs to its mother. The bhakti tradition exalts surrender above every other discipline, holding that the soul that abandons all self-reliance and clings to the divine is carried where its own effort could never bring it.

The cobbler Ravidas sings that even one of low birth, despised by the proud, becomes worthy through the love of the lord, and that the name lifts the lowliest above the high-born who lack it. The bhakti poets repeatedly proclaim that devotion overturns the orders of caste and station, for the divine, they sing, regards the heart and not the rank of the worshipper.

The poet sings that he has wasted his life in the marketplace of the world, buying and selling and forgetting the one thing needful, and that now, his hair grey, he turns at last to the name. The bhakti verses are often confessions of squandered time, and they urge the listener not to delay, for the body is a borrowed garment and the hour of remembrance will not wait.

The Tamil saints sang their love of the divine as they wandered from shrine to shrine, and their hymns, gathered into a sacred collection, describe the lord dwelling in each holy place and the rapture of beholding him. The poet declares that his eyes have melted at the sight, that his bones have softened, and that he can find no measure for the sweetness of the divine.

Surdas, blind from birth, sings of the child Krishna at play in the cowherd village, stealing butter and dancing in the dust, and the poet declares that though his outward eyes are dark, the inward eye beholds the lord at every moment. The bhakti tradition cherished the songs of the divine childhood, finding in the tender scenes a love that draws the heart more surely than the contemplation of majesty.

The poet sings that the divine name, repeated, is sweeter than nectar, that it cleanses the tongue that utters it and the ear that hears it, and that one moment spent in the company of those who love the name is worth more than an age of solitary austerity. The bhakti hymns make the recollection of the name the centre of the devotional life and the gathering of devotees its natural setting.

The poet asks the lord why he hides, why he lets the devotee call and call and gives no sign, and then answers his own complaint, saying that the hiding is itself a grace, for it deepens the longing and makes the soul cry out the more. The bhakti verses dwell often on the pain of separation, treating the ache of the absent beloved as a fire that purifies the heart.

The doctrine of the Trinity confesses one God in three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of one substance, equal in power and glory. The tradition insists that this is not a teaching of three gods, for the divine essence is one and undivided, nor a teaching of one person under three names, for the three are truly distinct, and the church has held this confession as the heart of its faith.

The theologians distinguish the persons of the Trinity by their relations of origin, the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten of the Father, the Spirit proceeding. These relations, they teach, do not divide the one essence but subsist within it, so that what distinguishes the persons is precisely their relation to one another, and the divine unity is not threatened by the distinction.

The baptismal command in the gospel, to baptise in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, was read by the church as a scriptural ground for the trinitarian confession. The interpreters noted that the word name stands in the singular though three are named, and they took this as a sign that the three are joined in a single divine reality into which the baptised are received.

Augustine, seeking analogies for the Trinity, looked into the structure of the human mind and found there a likeness in the mind that knows itself and loves itself, three and yet one. He offered the analogy with caution, knowing that no creature can fully image the creator, but he held that the soul, made in the divine image, bears some trace of the triune life of the God who made it.

The doctrine teaches that the works of the Trinity toward the creation are undivided, that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit act together in every divine act, and yet that each work may be attributed especially to one person. Creation is referred to the Father, redemption to the Son, sanctification to the Spirit, not because the others are absent but because each work befits the person to whom it is ascribed.

The Cappadocian theologians clarified the trinitarian language by distinguishing the one thing that the three share, the divine essence, from the three that each is, the persons. They taught that there is one essence in three persons, and this precise vocabulary allowed the church to affirm both the unity and the distinction without collapsing either, and it became the standard grammar of the doctrine.

The Eastern tradition speaks of the mutual indwelling of the three persons, each wholly in the others, a coinherence so complete that to see one is to see the others and to act is to act as one. The image offered is of three lamps in a single room whose lights so interpenetrate that no beam can be assigned to one alone, and yet the lamps remain three.

The doctrine of the Trinity arose, the theologians have held, not from speculation but from the church's effort to be faithful to its scriptures and its worship at once. The scriptures called the Father God, called the Son God, called the Spirit God, and yet confessed one God, and the worship of the church addressed the three; the doctrine is the church's attempt to hold all that it had received without surrendering any part.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. The apostle's closing greeting, naming the three together in a single blessing, was treasured by the church as an early witness to the trinitarian faith, and the interpreters found in its order and its rhythm a confession woven into the texture of the apostolic letters.

The theologians have insisted that the Trinity is a mystery in the strict sense, a truth that exceeds the reach of unaided reason and is known only because it has been revealed. They have offered analogies and clarified the language, but they have warned that the analogies limp and the language only guards the mystery rather than dissolving it, and that the proper end of trinitarian reflection is worship rather than comprehension.

Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. The version of the beatitudes that addresses the hearers directly is followed by a series of woes, woe to you who are rich, who are full, who laugh now, and the pairing sharpens the reversal that the blessing announces.

The scriptures repeatedly declare that God hears the cry of the poor, that he raises the needy from the dust and lifts the beggar from the ash heap to set him among princes. The song of the woman who would bear the prophet, and later the song of the mother of Jesus, both sing of a God who scatters the proud and exalts the lowly, filling the hungry and sending the rich away empty.

The law of Israel made provision for the poor in the very ordering of the harvest, commanding the owner of a field not to reap to the edges and not to gather the gleanings, but to leave them for the poor and the sojourner. The forgotten sheaf left in the field was likewise to be left, and the scriptures ground these provisions in the memory that the people themselves had been slaves and aliens.

The prophets denounce those who trample the head of the poor into the dust and who buy the needy for a pair of sandals, and they declare that the festivals and offerings of such a people are an offence. The scriptural concern for the poor is not a marginal theme but stands at the centre of the prophetic indictment, the treatment of the powerless being made the test of the nation's faithfulness.

Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom? The letter of James presses the question against a congregation that had shown deference to the well-dressed visitor and contempt for the poor one, and it reads the favour of God toward the poor as a rebuke to the partiality that the church had let creep into its assemblies.

The first beatitude has come down in two forms, one blessing the poor in spirit and one blessing simply the poor, and the interpreters have read the two together rather than choosing between them. The poverty the beatitude commends, on this reading, is at once an outward condition and an inward disposition, the emptiness of hand and the emptiness of self-reliance that leaves room for the kingdom.

The Quran joins the care of the poor to the very definition of piety, declaring that righteousness is to give of one's wealth, despite love for it, to the kinsfolk, the orphans, the needy, the traveller, and those who ask. The obligatory share set aside from wealth for the poor is named among the pillars of the faith, so that the scripture binds devotion to God to the relief of the destitute.

Truly I tell you, the gospel records Jesus saying, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me. The teaching of the judgment of the nations makes the welcome of the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick, and the prisoner the criterion of the verdict, and it identifies the divine king himself with the poor who were served or neglected.

The year of jubilee, commanded in the law, returned the land to its original families and freed those who had fallen into servitude, so that no household would be permanently dispossessed. The provision treats poverty not as a fixed fate but as a condition the community is bound to undo at the appointed time, and the scripture grounds the law in the declaration that the land belongs to God and the people are his tenants.

Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. The interpreters have noted that the beatitude takes up the words of a psalm that promises the land to the meek while the wicked are cut off, and they have read the meek not as the timid but as those who do not grasp, who renounce the violent seizure of what they want and so receive, as a gift, what the grasping lose.

The Master said that at fifteen he set his heart on learning, at thirty he stood firm, at forty he had no doubts, at fifty he knew the decree of heaven, at sixty his ear was obedient, and at seventy he could follow what his heart desired without overstepping the bounds. The Analects records this account of a lifetime's growth as a measure of the moral self-cultivation the tradition holds before the learner.

Do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself. So the Master answered the disciple who asked for a single word that might serve as a rule for the whole of life, and he named it reciprocity.
