The Analects returns often to this principle, treating the imaginative placing of oneself in the position of the other as the root of humane conduct.

The Master said that if the people are guided by laws and kept in order by punishments, they will avoid wrongdoing but have no sense of shame; if they are guided by virtue and kept in order by ritual, they will have a sense of shame and will moreover become good. The Analects sets the formative power of ritual and example above the deterrent power of penalty.

The Book of Rites describes the ceremonies that order the relations of the family and the state, the rites of mourning and of sacrifice, of capping and of marriage, and it teaches that ritual is not empty form but the outward shape of an inward reverence. To perform the rite without the feeling, the classic warns, is hollow, and yet the feeling itself is schooled and given measure by the rite.

When the disciple asked about filial piety, the Master said that nowadays it is taken to mean merely the providing of food, but that even dogs and horses are given that; without reverence, what is the difference? The Analects treats the honour owed to parents as the first school of virtue, and it insists that the outward provision must be joined to an inward respect.

The Doctrine of the Mean teaches that what heaven has conferred is called the nature, that to follow the nature is called the way, and that the cultivation of the way is called instruction. The classic sets human conduct within a cosmic order, holding that the moral path is not an arbitrary code but the following of a nature given from above, and that the sage brings his life into accord with it.

The Great Learning teaches that the ancients who wished to illustrate virtue throughout the empire first ordered well their own states, and wishing to order their states they first regulated their families, and wishing to regulate their families they first cultivated their persons, and wishing to cultivate their persons they first rectified their hearts. The classic traces the ordering of the world back through a chain of disciplines to the rectifying of the inmost self.

The Master said that the noble person understands what is right, while the small person understands what is profitable. The Analects draws this contrast repeatedly, marking the noble person not by birth or rank but by the orientation of the will, the readiness to do what is fitting even at a cost, and the tradition holds this figure before the learner as the goal of the long labour of self-cultivation.

When the disciple Yan Hui asked about humane conduct, the Master said that to subdue the self and return to ritual is humane conduct, and that if a man could do this for a single day, the whole world would return to humaneness. The Analects ties the central virtue to the discipline of ritual, presenting the curbing of selfish impulse and the keeping of proper form as the path by which the heart is made humane.

The Master said that he transmitted but did not create, that he trusted in and loved the ancients. The Analects presents the teacher not as the founder of a new doctrine but as the faithful conveyor of an inherited wisdom, and the classics that the tradition gathered, the odes, the documents, the rites, and the changes, were valued as the deposit of that ancient teaching to be studied and handed on.

Then Peter came up and said, Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him, as many as seven times? Jesus said to him, I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven. The teaching sets no ceiling on forgiveness, and the parable of the unforgiving servant follows immediately, binding the mercy a person extends to the mercy he has himself received.

Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. The petition placed in the model prayer makes the forgiveness sought from God conditional, in some manner, on the forgiveness already granted to others, and the teaching that follows the prayer states it plainly, that if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not, neither will he.

The Quran counsels the believer to pardon and to overlook, asking whether one would not love that God should forgive him, and declaring that the recompense of an injury is an injury equal to it, but that whoever forgives and makes reconciliation will have his reward with God. The scripture permits the measured response but holds the way of pardon higher, joining forgiveness to the hope of divine mercy.

Joseph, revealing himself to the brothers who had sold him, told them not to be distressed or angry with themselves, for God had sent him before them to preserve life. The narrative offers one of the great scenes of forgiveness, the wronged one reframing the injury within a larger purpose and refusing to hold the offence against those who had done it.

The law of Israel forbade the bearing of a grudge and the taking of vengeance against the children of one's own people, and joined to the prohibition the command to love the neighbour as oneself. The interpreters have read the placing of the two together as a teaching that the love of neighbour begins with the refusal to nurse an injury, the letting go of the remembered wrong.

Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. The words spoken from the cross have been read by the tradition as the supreme enactment of the teaching on forgiveness, the wronged one praying for the wrongdoers in the very hour of the wrong, and the interpreters have found in the plea of ignorance a model for the charity that seeks the least culpable reading of an offence.

The day of atonement was established in the law as a yearly cleansing, on which the people afflicted themselves and the high priest made atonement for the sanctuary and the assembly, so that they might be clean from all their sins before the Lord. The provision set within the calendar a recurring occasion of pardon, a time appointed for the wiping away of the accumulated guilt of the year.

If your brother sins, the gospel instructs, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him; and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying I repent, you must forgive him. The teaching joins the readiness to forgive with the willingness to speak the truth about the wrong, so that forgiveness is not the pretence that no injury occurred but the release of the one who has done it.

If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. The teaching makes the repair of a broken relationship a precondition of acceptable worship, placing the duty of reconciliation even above the completion of the rite already begun.

Bear with one another, the apostle writes, and if one has a complaint against another, forgive each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. The pattern set throughout the scriptures grounds the obligation to forgive not in the deserving of the offender but in the prior mercy received, so that the forgiven are bound to become forgiving, and the unforgiving spirit is shown to contradict the grace it claims.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: All wisdom comes from the Lord and is with him forever. The opening of the book of Ben Sira places the source of wisdom in God and declares that the fear of the Lord is the beginning, the fullness, and the crown of wisdom. The sage gathers the practical counsel of a long tradition and binds it throughout to reverence, so that the shrewd observation of life is never severed from the worship of its maker.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: My child, the sage writes, if you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing. Set your heart right and be steadfast, and do not be impetuous in time of calamity. Cling to him and do not depart, that you may be honoured at the end of your life. The book of Ben Sira counsels the one who would be faithful to expect trial and to hold fast through it, promising that the testing refines rather than destroys.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: The book of Ben Sira praises the work of the physician and the medicines drawn from the earth, declaring that the Lord created them and that the skill of healing is itself a gift. Yet it counsels the sick to pray and to amend their lives along with seeking the physician's help, holding together the use of human craft and the dependence upon God in a single account of healing.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: Honour your father and forget not the birth pangs of your mother; remember that through your parents you were born, and what can you give back to them that equals their gift to you? The book of Ben Sira returns often to the duties of the household, and it teaches that the one who honours his father atones for sins and that kindness to a parent will not be forgotten in the day of need.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: Let us now praise famous men, the sage writes, and our fathers in their generations. The book of Ben Sira closes its instruction with a long hymn in honour of the ancestors, recalling the patriarchs, the lawgiver, the judges, the kings, and the prophets, and it teaches that their memory is a blessing and that their names live in the generations that come after them.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: The book of Ben Sira warns repeatedly about the power of the tongue, declaring that a slip on the pavement is better than a slip of the tongue, and that many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not so many as have fallen because of the tongue. The sage counsels the making of a balance and a scale for one's words, and the setting of a door and a bolt upon the mouth.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: A faithful friend is a sturdy shelter, the sage writes, and whoever finds one has found a treasure. There is nothing so precious as a faithful friend, and no scales can measure his excellence. The book of Ben Sira devotes careful counsel to friendship, teaching that a friend is tested in adversity, that a new friend is like new wine which must age before it is enjoyed, and that fidelity is the rarest and most valued of qualities.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: The book of Ben Sira teaches a measured generosity, counselling the giving of alms to the humble and the holding back from the scoffer, and it declares that a person's almsgiving is like a signet ring with the Lord and that he will keep a person's kindness like the apple of his eye. The sage joins the practice of charity to the trust that what is given to the poor is not lost but kept.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: Wisdom, in the book of Ben Sira, speaks in her own voice and tells how she came forth from the mouth of the Most High and sought a resting place among the nations, until the creator appointed her a dwelling in Israel and bade her take root among an honoured people. The sage identifies this wisdom with the law given through Moses, so that the cosmic figure and the covenant teaching are made one.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: The book of Ben Sira counsels reflection upon the last things, urging the reader in all that he does to remember the end of his life, and then he will never sin. The sage holds the thought of mortality before the mind not as a counsel of gloom but as a discipline of seriousness, a measure against the heedlessness that forgets the brevity of the days.

And the Lord said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters; I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them. The narrative of the deliverance opens with a God who has seen and heard and come down, and the whole sequence of plagues and the passage of the sea unfolds from this declared resolve to set the people free.

On the third new moon after the people had gone out of Egypt they came into the wilderness of Sinai, and the mountain was wrapped in smoke because the Lord had descended on it in fire. There were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud, and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled. The narrative frames the giving of the law as an encounter of overwhelming majesty.

The law given at the mountain is not the bare ten words alone but a body of ordinances regulating the treatment of servants, the goring ox, the kindled fire, the borrowed beast, the seduced maiden, and the resident alien. The narrative presents this case law as the working out of the covenant into the texture of daily life, so that the relationship sealed at Sinai reaches into every transaction.

While Moses was on the mountain the people grew impatient and made a calf of gold, and the narrative recounts the breaking of the tablets, the grinding of the calf to powder, and the intercession by which Moses pleaded for the people. The story of the law-giving thus includes the immediate breach of the covenant and the costly mending of it, the renewal of the tablets following upon the prophet's prayer.

And all the people answered together and said, all that the Lord has spoken we will do. The narrative records the people's assent before the full body of the law has been given, and the interpreters have read this as a teaching that the covenant is entered by trust, the people binding themselves to obedience in advance, on the strength of the deliverance already received.

The latter chapters of the narrative are given over to the instructions for the tabernacle, the dwelling that the people are to make so that the divine presence may go with them. The detailed prescriptions for the curtains, the ark, the lampstand, and the priestly garments have been read as a sign that the law-giving issues in worship, the covenant providing not only a code but a place of meeting.

The narrative records that when Moses came down from the mountain the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God, and the people were afraid to come near him. He put a veil over his face, removing it when he went in to speak with the Lord, and the interpreters have dwelt on this radiance as a sign of the transforming nearness of the one who gave the law.

Then Moses and Aaron and the elders went up, and they saw the God of Israel, and under his feet there was as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness. The narrative records that they beheld God and ate and drank, and the interpreters have read this meal upon the mountain as the ratification of the covenant, a banquet of the leaders in the divine presence.

The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, the narrative says, as a man speaks to his friend. Among all the figures of the deliverance the lawgiver is given a unique nearness to God, and the tradition has treasured this description, reading the friendship of Moses with the Lord as the ground of his authority and as a foreshadowing of the intimacy that the scriptures hold out to the faithful.

The Passover instituted on the night of the deliverance was commanded to be kept as a memorial throughout the generations, and the narrative provides for the child who will ask what the rite means, telling the parent to answer that it is the sacrifice of the Lord's passover. The law-giving thus includes the means of its own transmission, the rite carrying the story of deliverance forward into every household and every age.

The tantric scriptures teach a path in which the energies of the body, ordinarily the sources of bondage, are made the very means of liberation. The practitioner is instructed in the visualisation of deities, the recitation of seed syllables, and the sacred gestures of the hands, so that the senses and the imagination, rightly directed, become a vehicle for the realisation that the texts call the union of wisdom and method.

The tantric texts describe a subtle body of channels and centres along which a refined energy may be made to rise, and they teach that the practitioner who awakens this energy and conducts it through the centres attains states of consciousness inaccessible by ordinary means. The doctrine is held to be esoteric, transmitted only from a qualified teacher to a prepared disciple under vows of secrecy.

The tantric scriptures hold that the divine is at once transcendent and immanent in the world, and that the practitioner may worship the supreme reality under a particular form, the deity becoming the focus through which the formless is approached. The text guides the worshipper to identify with the visualised deity, dissolving the sense of a separate self, so that the worship culminates in the recognition of an original non-difference.

The tantric texts teach the use of the mandala, a diagram of the cosmos and of the assembly of deities, into which the practitioner enters in meditation as into a sacred precinct. The text describes the gates, the directions, and the throne at the centre, and it instructs the practitioner to construct the mandala in the mind and to dwell within it, treating the visualised palace as the dwelling of the awakened mind.

The tantric scriptures place great weight on the relationship between the teacher and the disciple, holding that the esoteric instruction cannot be received from a book alone but must be conferred through initiation. The text describes the rite by which the teacher empowers the disciple, opening the practice and binding the disciple to its vows, and it warns that the teaching pursued without this transmission is fruitless or even harmful.

The tantric texts speak of the mantra as a sound that carries power, not a mere sign but a vibration in which the deity is present. The practitioner is instructed to receive the mantra from the teacher, to recite it with attention to its rhythm and its meaning, and to let it pervade the mind until the boundary between the one who recites and the sound recited grows thin.

The tantric scriptures teach that the apparent opposition of the pure and the impure, the permitted and the forbidden, belongs to a lower understanding, and that the realised practitioner perceives a single reality pervading all things. Yet the texts surround this teaching with strict conditions, insisting that it is dangerous in the hands of one who has not been purified and prepared, and that it must remain veiled from the unready.

The tantric texts of the Buddhist tradition describe a path said to be swift, in which the practitioner takes the goal itself as the means, cultivating the awakened state in imagination before it is fully attained. The deity visualised is understood as the practitioner's own enlightened nature, and the practice is held to ripen, more rapidly than the ordinary path, the recognition of what was always present.

The tantric scriptures employ a deliberately veiled language, sometimes called the twilight language, in which words carry a hidden sense beyond their surface meaning. The text warns that the uninitiated reader who takes the words literally will misunderstand them entirely, and that the true import is disclosed only by the teacher, so that the secrecy is woven into the very wording of the texts.

The tantric texts conclude their instruction by directing the practitioner to dedicate the merit of the practice to the welfare of all beings, lest the powerful methods serve only the self. The dedication, the text teaches, turns the practice from a pursuit of private attainment into an act of compassion, and it is held to be the indispensable seal upon the whole esoteric path.

The book of Job refuses the easy doctrine that suffering is always the wage of sin. Job's friends press the explanation upon him, urging that he must have done wrong to be so afflicted, but the book vindicates Job against them, declaring at its close that they have not spoken rightly of God, while Job, who protested his innocence and demanded an answer, is the one who is honoured.

We rejoice in our sufferings, the apostle writes, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope. The passage does not deny the reality of the affliction but traces a path through it, holding that the hardship borne in trust is not wasted but works in the sufferer a transformation that issues in a hope which does not disappoint.

The Buddhist scriptures begin from the recognition of suffering as the first of the noble truths, declaring that birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, and that union with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant are suffering. Yet the same teaching declares a cessation, so that the unflinching naming of suffering is not despair but the first step of a path that leads beyond it.

The psalms of lament give the sufferer permission to bring the complaint itself before God, to ask how long and to ask why, and to set the grief into words rather than to suppress it. The scriptures thus include within worship the protest of the afflicted, treating the honest cry of pain not as a failure of faith but as a form of address that keeps the relationship open.

The Quran teaches that the believer will be tried with something of fear and hunger and the loss of wealth and lives and fruits, and it gives glad tidings to the patient, who, when struck by affliction, say that they belong to God and to him they return. The scripture sets the trials of life within a relationship of belonging, so that the loss is met not with mere stoicism but with a turning toward the one to whom all things return.

The fourth song of the servant in the prophet describes a figure who suffers not for his own wrongdoing but for the wrongdoing of others, who is wounded for their transgressions and by whose stripes they are healed. The passage opens a possibility that the older doctrine of retribution could not hold, that suffering may be borne on behalf of the many and may itself be the means of their restoration.

From the whirlwind God answers Job not with an explanation of his suffering but with a long survey of the creation, the foundations of the earth, the storehouses of the snow, the wild ass and the eagle and the great creatures of the deep. The answer does not solve the problem on Job's terms but enlarges the frame, and Job, having glimpsed a wisdom beyond his reckoning, falls silent and is comforted.

The book of Lamentations gives ritual form to a catastrophe, voicing the grief of a city laid waste and a people scattered, and it does not hurry to consolation. Yet in the middle of the dirge a single passage recalls that the steadfast love of the Lord never ceases and that his mercies are new every morning, so that even the most unrelieved of the scriptural laments holds open a thread of hope.

The gospels present the suffering of Jesus not as a defeat to be explained away but as the centre of the story, the way by which the saving work is accomplished. The teaching that the disciple must take up the cross and follow draws the suffering of the faithful into this pattern, holding that the path of discipleship runs through hardship and that the cross is not the contradiction of the way but its very shape.

The scriptures hold together the affirmation that God is good and the acknowledgement that the faithful suffer, and they do not resolve the tension into a tidy system. The book of Job leaves the deepest question unanswered in the terms in which it was asked, and the tradition has read this reticence as a teaching that suffering is to be borne in trust rather than dissolved by a theory, the sufferer sustained by a relationship rather than an explanation.

The scriptures of more than one tradition describe the world as brought into being by a deliberate ordering rather than emerging from chaos by chance. The Genesis account moves from a formless void to a structured cosmos, the waters divided, the dry land gathered, the lights set in the firmament, and the refrain that it was good marks each stage as the realisation of a design.

The Quran describes the heavens and the earth as joined together before God parted them, and it speaks of the seven heavens raised without pillars that can be seen, and of the sun and moon each running its appointed course. The scripture presents the order of the cosmos as a sign for those who reflect, the regularity of the celestial motions pointing the observer toward the wisdom of the maker.

The hymn of the cosmic person in the Vedic scriptures describes the world as fashioned from the sacrifice of a primal being, the sky from his head, the earth from his feet, the sun from his eye, the orders of society from his limbs. The cosmology presents the universe as the body of a single reality, every part of the visible world bearing a relation to the whole from which it came.

The wisdom literature pictures the creation as the work of a divine wisdom present at the founding of the world, beside the creator as a master craftsman when he marked out the foundations of the earth and assigned the sea its limit. The cosmos, on this reading, is not a brute fact but the expression of an intelligence, and its order is the trace of the wisdom by which it was made.

The scriptures describe a creation that is declared good and yet entrusted to the care of the creatures within it. The human being is set in the garden to work it and keep it, and the dominion granted is read by the interpreters as a stewardship rather than a licence, the creation order placing humanity within the world as its tender rather than above it as its owner.

The psalms turn the contemplation of the cosmos into praise, calling the heavens to declare the glory of God and the firmament to proclaim the work of his hands. The scripture reads the day and the night as a speech without words, a testimony poured forth through all the earth, so that the order of the creation is itself a kind of utterance addressed to whoever will attend.

The scriptures describe the heavens as the dwelling of God and the throne of his majesty, and the earth as his footstool, and yet they qualify the image, for the prophet asks what house could be built for the one whom the highest heaven cannot contain. The cosmology thus holds together the picture of an ordered creation and the affirmation that the creator infinitely exceeds it.

The Genesis narrative places the creation of the human being on the same day as the land animals and yet sets it apart by a deliberate counsel and the conferral of the divine image. The creation order, in this reading, joins humanity to the rest of the living world as a creature among creatures while marking a distinct vocation, so that kinship and calling are held together.

The scriptures speak of a creation that is not yet complete but is moving toward a fulfilment, the seventh day of rest pointing beyond the work of making toward a consummation. The prophets and the apostolic writings extend this forward movement, holding that the whole creation waits with eager longing, so that the cosmology of the scriptures is bound to a hope of renewal.

The opening of the Gospel of John takes up the language of the creation narrative, declaring that in the beginning was the Word and that all things were made through him. The interpreters have read this as a teaching that the same wisdom by which the cosmos was ordered is the Word made flesh, so that the creation order and the work of redemption are bound to a single source.

Job, in the depth of his affliction, does not curse God as his wife urges, but neither does he accept the verdict of his friends. He insists that he will hold fast his integrity and will argue his case to the divine face, declaring that though God slay him, yet will he trust, and even so will he defend his ways before him. The book honours this refusal to confess a guilt he does not feel.

The friends of Job advance the doctrine of exact retribution, that the righteous prosper and the wicked are punished, and they reason backward from Job's suffering to a hidden sin. The book sets their long and eloquent speeches against the reader's knowledge, given in the opening chapters, that Job is blameless, so that the friends' theology is heard from the start as a structure that cannot hold the case before it.

I know that my redeemer lives, Job declares in the midst of his complaint, and that at the last he will stand upon the earth, and that after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God. The verse rises out of the darkest part of the book, a flash of confidence amid the protest, and the tradition has treasured it as a witness to a hope that the suffering could not extinguish.

The book of Job frames the question of innocent suffering with a scene in the heavenly court, where the accuser proposes that Job serves God only for the benefits he receives. The wager that follows asks whether disinterested faith is possible, whether a person will hold to God when every reward is stripped away, and the book's drama turns on whether Job's devotion will survive the loss of all that might be thought to motivate it.

When God finally speaks to Job from the whirlwind, the long-awaited answer is not a defence of the divine justice but a series of questions that Job cannot answer. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades? The interpreters have read this response as a refusal of the terms of the debate, an enlargement of Job's vision rather than a verdict in his case.

At the end of the book Job answers that he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear, but that now his eye sees him, and that therefore he despises himself and repents in dust and ashes. The interpreters have asked what Job repents of, since the book has declared him blameless, and many have read the repentance not as a confession of the friends' charge but as the surrender of his demand for an explanation.

The book of Job ends by declaring that the friends have not spoken of God what is right, as Job has, and the verdict has long puzzled the interpreters, since Job said many bitter things. The traditional reading holds that Job is vindicated not for the accuracy of his words but for the honesty of his address, for speaking to God rather than merely about him, while the friends defended a doctrine and missed the man.

The figure of the divine speeches dwells at length on the wild creatures, the lion and the raven, the wild ox that will not serve, the ostrich that deals cruelly with her young, the great beasts that no human hand can tame. The interpreters have read this catalogue as a teaching that the creation is wider and stranger than the moral order the friends had imagined, and that its wisdom is not exhausted by the reckoning of reward and punishment.

Naked I came from my mother's womb, Job says when the news of his losses reaches him, and naked shall I return; the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. The book records this as the first response to catastrophe, an acceptance that the later chapters will strain and complicate but never wholly abandon, the wrestling that follows growing out of a devotion that the loss did not at once destroy.

The book of Job has been read across the traditions as the scripture that refuses every premature consolation, that lets the sufferer rage and question without condemning him, and that ends not with an answer to the problem of evil but with an encounter. The interpreters have held that the book's wisdom lies in this very restraint, the willingness to leave the hardest question open while affirming that the questioner is not abandoned.

A brother came to one of the elders and asked for a word, and the old man said to him, go and sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything. The sayings of the desert fathers, gathered into collections, preserve such brief counsels, and the recurring instruction to remain in the cell teaches that the discipline of staying put is itself a school of the soul.

A young monk asked an elder why, though he prayed, his heart remained dry. The old man said that the water wears away the stone not by its force but by its constancy, drop after drop, and that so the soul is softened not by a single great prayer but by the patient repetition of the small ones. The desert sayings teach perseverance over intensity.

An elder was asked what he did all day in the desert, and he answered that he fell down and rose again, fell down and rose again, without ceasing. The desert sayings hold no expectation of an unbroken progress; they teach instead that the spiritual life is a matter of rising once more after each fall, and that the one who keeps rising is not defeated.

A brother sinned, and the council called an elder to come and judge him, but he refused. When pressed, he came carrying a leaking basket of sand behind him, and he said that his own sins were running out behind him and he did not see them, yet he had come to judge the sins of another. The desert sayings use such enacted parables to teach the relinquishing of judgment.

An old man said that the monk must be like a person who is dead, who is not stirred by insult or by praise, who is indifferent to honour and to contempt, for the dead do not answer back. The desert sayings teach a freedom from the opinion of others, holding that the soul is enslaved as long as it is moved by the wish to be esteemed and the fear of being despised.

A brother asked an elder how he might be saved, and the old man took off his cloak, girded himself, and stretched out his hands to heaven, saying that the monk, if he wills, may become wholly like a flame. The desert sayings present the spiritual life not as a moderate adjustment but as a total offering, the whole self given up to the fire of love.

An elder taught that the beginning of the soul's healing is to keep watch over the thoughts, for the deed is the fruit of the thought, and the one who lets a wandering thought grow unchecked will find it bearing him away. The desert sayings devote much attention to the discernment of thoughts, teaching the monk to recognise the suggestion at its first rising and to turn from it before it takes hold.

A brother asked an elder whether it was better to fast strictly or to keep the rule of hospitality and eat with a visiting guest. The old man said that to break the fast for the sake of love is no fault, for fasting is a tool and love is the work, and the desert sayings repeatedly subordinate the outward austerities to the charity they are meant to serve.

An old man said that if a person held the remembrance of death always before his eyes, he would never sin, for the awareness of the brief and uncertain span would burn away the heedlessness in which wrongdoing grows. The desert sayings counsel this remembrance not as a morbid dwelling on mortality but as a discipline that gives weight and seriousness to each passing hour.

A brother asked an elder for a word of salvation, and the old man was silent a long while, then said only that he should forgive his neighbour, and the neighbour would be forgiven, and so the brother himself would be forgiven. The desert sayings, for all the severity of their askesis, return again and again to this simple root, that the gate of mercy opens for the one who has opened it for another.

Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. The teaching grounds the practice of prayer in the assurance of a hearing, and it follows the promise with the image of a father who will not give a stone to a child who asks for bread.

The scriptures teach that prayer should be persistent, and the parable of the widow who wears down the unjust judge by her continual coming makes the point by contrast: if even an unjust judge will yield to persistence, how much more will the God who is just hear the cry of his own. The teaching urges the one who prays not to lose heart when the answer is delayed.

The Psalter is itself a school of prayer, gathering the whole range of the soul's address to God, the cry of distress and the shout of praise, the confession of sin and the protest of innocence, the lament of the abandoned and the thanksgiving of the delivered. The tradition has read the psalms as words given for the worshipper to take up, so that the one who has no words of his own may pray in the words of the scripture.

The Quran teaches that God is near and answers the call of the one who calls upon him, and it instructs the believer to call upon his Lord humbly and in secret, for he does not love the transgressors. The scripture joins the assurance of nearness to a counsel of humility, holding that prayer is the act by which the servant acknowledges his dependence and turns toward the one on whom he depends.

When you pray, the teaching instructs, do not heap up empty phrases as the pagans do, who think they will be heard for their many words; for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. The instruction frees the one who prays from the anxiety of eloquence, holding that prayer is not the persuading of a reluctant power but the address of a child to a father who already knows.

The apostle instructs the believers to pray without ceasing, to rejoice always, and to give thanks in all circumstances. The counsel has been read not as a command to be always saying words but as a charge to cultivate a continual orientation of the heart toward God, so that prayer becomes less an interruption of life than the atmosphere in which the whole of life is carried on.

The scriptures record prayers of intercession in which one person stands before God on behalf of others, Abraham pleading for the city, Moses interceding for the people who had sinned, the prophet praying for those who had wronged him. The tradition has read these scenes as a teaching that prayer reaches beyond the one who prays, and that to bear another before God is among the highest forms of love.

We do not know what to pray for as we ought, the apostle writes, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. The passage acknowledges the poverty of the one who prays, the not knowing even what to ask, and it locates the help not in a better technique but in a divine assistance that takes up the inarticulate longing and carries it where it could not go alone.

In the garden before his death, the gospel records, Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from him, and then added the words, yet not what I will, but what you will. The tradition has read this prayer as the pattern of all petition, the honest naming of the desire of the heart held within a final surrender to the will of God, so that prayer asks freely and yet entrusts the outcome.

The scriptures join prayer to the forgiveness of others and to the setting right of wrongs, teaching that the hands lifted in prayer must be clean and that the worshipper who comes to the altar must first be reconciled with his brother. Prayer, on this teaching, is not sealed off from conduct but bound to it, and a life at odds with the neighbour cannot offer an undivided heart to God.

He has told you, O man, what is good, and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God. The prophet places humility at the close of his summary of the divine requirement, and the interpreters have read the walking humbly as the inward disposition without which the doing of justice and the loving of kindness lose their root.

The parable of the two who went up to the temple to pray sets the proud prayer of one who recounted his merits against the lowly prayer of one who would not lift his eyes but only asked for mercy. Jesus declared that the second went home justified rather than the first, for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.

Have this mind among yourselves, the apostle writes, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. The hymn of self-emptying is held out as the pattern of humility, the lowering of the self for the sake of others grounded in the descent of the one who is praised.

When Jesus had washed the feet of his disciples, an office belonging to a servant, he said that he had given them an example, that they also should do as he had done. The scene has been read by the tradition as the enacted teaching of humility, the master taking the lowest place so that the disciples might learn that greatness in the kingdom is measured by service.

God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. The apostolic writers quote this saying from the older scriptures and draw from it a counsel to humble oneself under the mighty hand of God, holding that the lowly heart is the one to which grace can be given, since pride closes the hand that humility opens to receive.

The Quran describes the servants of the Merciful as those who walk upon the earth in humility, and who, when the ignorant address them harshly, answer with words of peace. The scripture sets humility not as weakness but as a settled gentleness, a refusal to meet provocation with provocation, and it counts this bearing among the marks of the truly devout.

When the disciples argued about who was the greatest, Jesus took a child and set the child among them, saying that whoever would be first must be last of all and servant of all, and that unless they turned and became like children they would not enter the kingdom. The teaching makes the lowliness of a child, who claims no rank, the very condition of entry.

When you are invited to a feast, the teaching counsels, do not sit down in the place of honour, lest one more distinguished than you arrive and you be asked to move down in shame; but sit in the lowest place, so that you may be invited higher. The instruction reads as worldly prudence and yet carries a deeper lesson, that the one who does not grasp at honour is the one to whom honour may be given.

Moses is described in the scriptures as very humble, more than all the people who were on the face of the earth, and the tradition has found it striking that the greatest of the prophets, who spoke with God face to face, should be marked above all by this quality. The interpreters have read the pairing as a teaching that true nearness to God produces not pride but a deepening lowliness.

The Buddhist scriptures count conceit among the fetters that bind the mind, the subtle insistence on the self that persists even where grosser faults have fallen away. The discourses teach that the comparing of oneself with others, whether to claim superiority, equality, or inferiority, springs from the same root, and that the freed mind has laid down the measuring of the self altogether.
